en: 1.1: The traditional collection has been handed down; it is now to be explained. 1.1:
This very collection is called the *Nighaṇṭus*. 1.1: Why are they called *Nighaṇṭus*? Because these are the *nigamas* (Vedic citations).

1,1: Having been collected again and again from the *chandasaḥ* (Vedic meters), they have been handed down [in this text]. Aupamanyava says that although they are indeed *nigantavaḥ* (derived from verbal roots), they are called *nighaṇṭavaḥ* because of their being "collected" (*nigamanāt*).
Alternatively, they may be so called because of "striking" (*hananāt*), for they are indeed struck together.

1.1: Or rather, when they have been collected together—those which are these four classes of words (*padajātāni*), namely nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and particles (*nipāta*)—they are as follows. Among them, they provide this definition for nouns and verbs.

1.1: A verb has action as its primary meaning; nouns have substance as their primary meaning. Thus, when both [the verb and the noun] have action as their primary meaning—as in "he goes" (*vrajati*) or "he cooks" (*pacati*)—one expresses through the verb an action that is characterized by temporal sequence (prior and posterior).
1.1: From its commencement until its completion, that which is embodied and has become a being is designated by the names of "beings" (*sattva*), such as "going" or "cooking. 1.1:
"This" is the designation for beings, such as "cow," "horse," "man," or "elephant. 1.1:
"It exists" is the designation for a state of being (*bhāva*), such as "he sits," "he lies down," "he goes," or "he stands."

1,1: Audumbarāyaṇa [maintains] that speech is eternal in its constituent elements (*indriya*). 1,2: In that case, however, a fourfold division is not logically tenable. 1,2: Furthermore, there would be mutual instruction among sounds produced either non-simultaneously or simultaneously, as well as the application [of grammatical rules] established by the treatise (*śāstra*).
1.2: Because it possesses pervasiveness and because it is subtler than sound, the designation "sound" (śabda) is established for the sake of worldly usage.
1.2: The deities are designated by means of words just as humans are.
1.2: Since the knowledge of the person (puruṣavidyā) is not eternal, the accomplishment of the ritual action is achieved through the mantra in the Veda.
1.2: "There are six modifications of being," says Vārṣyāyaṇi:
"it is born, it exists, it transforms, it grows, it declines, and it perishes.
Regarding the term "is born," it expresses the beginning of a prior state; it does not express a subsequent state, nor does it negate it.
1,2: "It exists" is the determination of a being that has arisen;
1,2: "it transforms" is the modification [of something] that does not fall away from its essence;
1,2: "it grows" is the accumulation of its own limbs, or the increase of things belonging to its own class.
"1,2: It increases through victory," or "it increases through the body.
1,2: "It diminishes" is explained by this very same [process] in reverse.
1,2: "It perishes" expresses the beginning of a subsequent state; it does not express a prior state, nor does it negate it.

1.3: "Other modifications of being are merely variations of these [three]; so it has been said. They are to be inferred according to their verbal expression. 1.3: "Prefixes do not express meanings independently," says Śākaṭāyana;
rather, they serve to illuminate the connection with the action of the noun or the verb.
1,3: "The meanings of words are high and low," says Gārgya.

1,3: Regarding those meanings of words, they say that this [distinction] is the modification of the meaning of nouns (*nāman*) and verbs (*ākhyāta*). 1,3: *Ā* is used in the sense of "nearby" (*arvāk*); *pra* and *parā* are its opposites.

1,3: *abhi* and *iti* signify "facing toward" (*ābhimukhya*); *prati* and *iti* signify the opposite of this. 1,3: *ati* and *su* signify "highly honored" (*abhipūjita*); *nir* and *dur* signify the opposite of these. 1,3: *ni* and *ava* signify "restraint" (*vinigraha*); *ud* and *iti* signify the opposite of these.
*Sam-* signifies unification; *vy-ap-* signifies the opposite of that;
*anv-* signifies similarity and posteriority;
*api-* signifies conjunction.
1.3: *upa* signifies proximity; 1.3: *pari* signifies being on all sides;
1.3: *adhi* signifies being above or sovereignty.
1,3: Thus, those who speak of high and low meanings should be disregarded. 1,4: Now, particles (nipāta) fall upon high and low meanings;
they serve as comparisons, they serve to include an object, and they serve to complete a metrical foot.
1.4: These four function as particles of comparison for them:
*iva*, both in common speech and in the Vedic texts. For example: *agnir iva* (ṚV X.84.2; 106.3) and *indra iva* (ṚV X.84.5; 166.2; 173.2).

1.4: *na* is a particle expressing negation (*pratiṣedha-artha*) in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), and it follows both [the verb and the preceding word] throughout the study of the Veda. 1.4: In the passage, "They did not consider Indra as a god" (Ṛgveda X.86.1), *na* expresses negation. 1.4: Its usage is such that it precedes that which it negates.
1.4: "Like those intoxicated by wine" (ṚV V.21.2.12)—this [particle] has the sense of a comparison.
1.4: The subsequent usage [of the particle] is that by which one makes a comparison.
1.4: The word *cit* has many functions; when used in the sense of honor, as in "the teacher might even say this," it expresses respect.

1.4: Why is he called an *ācārya*? An *ācārya* is so called because he causes one to grasp right conduct (*ācāra*), or because he gathers (*ācinoti*) meanings, or because he gathers wisdom (*buddhi*).
1.4: In the phrase *dadhi cit*, the word *cit* is used in the sense of a comparison (*upamā*).
1.4: In the phrase *kulmāṣāṃś cit āhara*, the word *cit* is used in the sense of contempt (*avakutsita*).

1.4: *Kulmāṣāḥ* means "they sit in the houses. 1.4: *Nu* has many functions; it is used as a statement of reason when one says, "He will do this now," or "How indeed will he do it? when asked, and also "Did he not indeed do that? Furthermore, it is also used in the sense of comparison (*upamā*).
1,4: "O you who are invoked by many, your branches are like those of a tree" (Ṛgveda V 1,24,3).
1,4: O you who are invoked by many, your branches are like the branches of a tree;
branches are so called because they move with the wind.

1.4: The branches are "khaśayas" because they are capable (*śaknoti*) [of being grasped]. 1.4: Now, that which is understood as a distinct meaning through its derivation (*āgama*), and not merely as a formal designation (*auddeśika*) due to its distinctness in analysis (*vigraha*), is the "inclusion of the object" (*karmopasaṃgraha*). 1.4: The particle *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) and is employed with both [the preceding and the following].
In this very sense, [the word] "ca" occurs in *Ṛgveda* V.21.62.11: "I and you, O slayer of Vṛtra";
and the vowel "ā" occurs in *Ṛgveda* X.16.11: "from the gods and from the ancestors.
The particle "vā" is used in the sense of deliberation (*vicāra*).
1,4: "Come, I shall place this earth here or there" (RV X.119.9).
1,4: Furthermore, it occurs in the sense of a conjunction (samuccaya), as in: 1,5: "Whether Vāyu [placed] you, or Manu [placed] you" (TS 1.7.7.2; KS 13.14).
1.5: *Aha* and *iti ha* are used in the sense of restriction (*vinigraha*) when joined with what precedes them; for example:
"Let this person do this," or "This one will do this, but that one will not do it.
Furthermore, the particle *u* is also used in this same sense when joined with what follows.
1,5: "They speak falsehood; they indeed speak the truth. 1,5: Furthermore, it serves as a verse-filler (*padapūraṇa*), as in "idam u" (RV 10.51.1) and "tad u" (RV 1.62.6).
1,5: For "hi" is this [particle] which has many functions; 1,5: it is used in the indication of a reason in the sense of "for he will do this";
1,5: and when asked, "How indeed will he do it? [it is used to answer].
1.5: *katham hi vyākariṣyati* is used in the sense of censure (*asūyā*). 1.5: *kila* is used in the sense of excellence of knowledge (*vidyā-prakarṣa*), as in *evam kila*.
1.5: It is also employed when not previously questioned, in conjunction with *atha api na* and *nanu*.
*na kila evam* and *nanu kila evam*;
*mā* is used for prohibition, as in *mā kārṣīḥ* and *mā hārṣīḥ*;
*khalu* is used as *khalu kṛtvā* and *khalu kṛtam*.
1,5: Furthermore, *atha api* is used for the sake of completing the meter; *evaṃ khalu tad babhūva iti*.
1,5: *Śaśvat* is used in the common language (*bhāṣā*) to express doubt;
*śaśvad evam* is used when there has been no prior inquiry.
1,5: *evam* and *śaśvat* are used when not asked by oneself;
1,5: *nūnam* is used in the colloquial language (*bhāṣā*) to express doubt; 1,5: both *anvadhyāyam* and *nūnam* are used to express doubt and as word-fillers (*padapūraṇa*).
1.5: Having prepared the oblation for Indra, Agastya desired to offer it to the Maruts.
Indra came and lamented: 1.6:
"There is nothing now, nor will there be anything tomorrow; who knows that which is mysterious? (Ṛgveda 1.170.1).
1,6: "The mind of another is to be moved by influence; even what has been studied perishes" (ṚV 1,170,1).
1,6: Truly, there is nothing for today, nor indeed anything for tomorrow. 1,6: On this very day.
1.6: *Dyu* is the name for the day, because it shines (*dyotate*). 1.6: *Śvas* is the time to be praised;

*hyas* is the past time. 1.6: "Who knows that which is wondrous? Who knows that which has come into being? (Ṛgveda 10.129.6). 1.6: "Who knows that which is marvelous? Who knows that which has become? (Ṛgveda 10.129.7).
1,6: This other [matter] also is a marvel, as if it were unprecedented:
"The mind of another is to be moved by influence. One who moves [it] cannot be led away;
for *citta* is derived from the root *cit* (to perceive/think).

1,6: Regarding the phrase "even what has been studied perishes," it is intended that even what has been studied [the Veda] perishes; furthermore, it is also used for the purpose of completing the meter. 1,7:
"Surely that wealthy sacrificial fee of yours, O Indra, shall yield its reward to the singer as a boon" (Ṛgveda 2.11.21).
1,7: "May there be skill for the singers; may Bhaga not fail us. May we, with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly" (Ṛgveda 2.11.21).
1,7: This is the boon milked out for you from the progenitor. 1,7: A boon is that which is to be chosen.
1,7: The singer and the one who causes to sing;
1,7: The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), which is wealthy and bountiful; 1,7: "Magha" is a name for wealth, derived from the root *maṃhati*, meaning the act of giving.

1.7: *Dakṣiṇā* is derived from the root *dakṣ*, meaning "to prosper"; it causes the deficiency of a ritual action to be made complete. Alternatively, it is so called because of the movement toward the right.
Intending the [southern] direction, the hand whose nature is that of the direction is the *dākṣiṇa* (right) hand.

1,7: [The word *dakṣa*] may derive from the root *dakṣ*, meaning "to exert effort," or from *dāś*, "to give. 1,7: *Hasta* comes from the root *han*, "to strike"; *prāśu* refers to striking. 1,7: Grant desires to the worshippers.
1,7: Do not abandon us;
1,7: Do not pass us by and give [to others]; 1,7: May Bhaga be ours.
1,7: "May we speak aloud in our own dwelling. 1,7: "Bhaga" [is derived] from the root *bhaj* (to distribute/share).
1,7: "Bṛhat" is a name for the Great; it is that which has become fully grown (*parivṛḍha*). (Note: *parivṛḍham* is read as *parivṛḍham* by Bhāskara.)
1,7: *vīravantaḥ* means "possessing excellent heroes" (*kalyāṇavīrāḥ*).

1,7: A hero (*vīraḥ*) is so called because he exerts himself against enemies (*amitrān vīrayati*), or it may derive from the root *vī* meaning "to go," or from the root *vīrayati*. 1,7: *sīm* has the sense of inclusion (*parigraha*) or is a word-filler (*padapūraṇa*).
1,7: "The Āditya emitted it" (ṚV 2.28.4).
Regarding this, [the word] *prāsṛjat* means either "he emitted" or "he emitted from all sides. And also:
"From there, Vena brought forth the far-shining one" (AV 4.1.1; 5.6.1; ŚV 1.321; Vṣ 13.3).
1,7: The Āditya has opened [the door] on all sides;
1,7: the beautiful rays of the Āditya shine forth due to their splendor;
or rather, one may take the word *sīmā* as a meaningless suffix added to the fifth case form of the object.

1,7: *sīmnaḥ*, *sīmataḥ*, *sīmātaḥ*, *maryādātaḥ* (from the boundary). 1,7: "The boundary (*sīmā*) and the limit (*maryādā*) bind together the two regions. 1,7: The pronoun *tva-*, used for the purpose of restriction, is unaccented; some say it is a partial name (*ardhanāman*).
1,8: "One sits nourishing the growth of the *ṛc*s, while another sings the *gāyatra* on the *śakvarī* verses" (ṚV X.71.11).
1,8: "One speaks as a *brahmán* with knowledge of what has been born, while another measures out the proportions of the sacrifice" (ṚV X.71.11).
Thus, [the text] declares the distribution of the duties of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
1.8: One, having nourished them, sits as the Hotṛ priest, increasing the abundance of the Ṛcs; the Ṛc is that which is to be praised.
1.8: Another, the Udgātṛ, sings the Gāyatra upon the Śakvarī verses.
The word "Gāyatra" is derived from the root *gai*, meaning "to praise."
1.8: The *śakvarī* verses [are so called] from the root *śak* (to be able).
It is known from scripture: "Because by means of these [verses] he was able (*aśakat*) to slay Vṛtra, that is the reason for the *śakvarī* nature of the *śakvarīs*" (KB 23.2;
AB 5.7.3). 1.8: The *brahman* priest alone proclaims the sacred knowledge at every birth [of a child].

1.8: Brahmā is all-knowing; he is capable of knowing everything. 1.8: Brahmā is preeminent through sacred learning; he is preeminent in every respect. 1.8: He alone measures out the dimensions of the sacrifice.

1,8: *Adhvaryu*, *adhvaryu*: he who goes to the sacrifice (*adhvara-yu*) yokes the sacrifice; he is the leader of the sacrifice, or he desires the sacrifice. Alternatively, the suffix *-yu* is attached to the present participle. "Sacrifice" (*adhvara*) is a name for the ritual; for the root *dhvarati* means "to injure," and it is the negation of that [injury].

1.8: Some say [the word *sakhye*] is a particle (*nipāta*). How then could it be a noun (*nāman*) whose original form is unaccented (*anudātta-prakṛti*), yet its case-ending is observed? For example, in the second case: "uta tvam sakhye sthirapītam āhuḥ" (ṚV X.71.5);
and in the fourth case: "uto tvasmai tanvaṃ visastre" (ṚV X.71.4).
1,8: Now, furthermore, regarding the nominative plural:
1,9: "Friends endowed with eyes and endowed with ears have become unequal in the swiftness of their thoughts" (ṚV X.71.7).
1,9: "Some appear like ponds reaching to the mouth or to the armpits; others appear as if for bathing" (ṚV X.71.7).

1,9: "Friends possessed of eyes and ears. 1,9: "Because of the casting of the eye and because of the anointing," says Āgrāyaṇa. 1,9: "Therefore these two appear as it were more distinct," so it is understood from a tradition whose source is untraced.

1,9: Karṇa derives from the root *kṛt* (to cut); thus it has its openings cut out. Āgrāyaṇa says it derives from the root *ṛcch* (to go). It is known from scripture: "They seem to go toward the sky as they rise up. 1,9: In their mental impulses, some were unequal; others reached up to the mouth, while others reached up to the armpits.

1,9: *Āsya* is from the root *asyati*; it means "this food flowed forth. 1,9: *Daghnam* is from the root *daghyate*; it flows from the action of the root *das*, or it may be that which becomes more widely known (*vidastatara*). 1,9: Some appeared like lakes fit for bathing; they appeared as those worthy of bathing (*prasneyā*). (The variant reading is: *prasneyā dadṛśire*). They are worthy of bathing.
1,9: *hradaḥ* may be derived from the root *hrād*, meaning "to sound," or from *hlād*, meaning "to become cool. 1,9:
Furthermore, it occurs in the sense of a conjunction:
"Your *āśvina* [cup] is as if a synonym [of the others]. (Ṛgveda-Brāhmaṇa 17,4).

1.9: [The sections] beginning with "The Āśvina and the Paryāyas. 1.9: Now, those particles (*nipāta*) which occur as sentence-fillers (*vākya-pūraṇa*) in treatises of unlimited syllables when the sense has already been established are meaningless (*anarthaka*) in treatises of limited syllables; they are *kam*, *īm*, *id*, and *u*. 1.10: "O men, even one who is toothless and breathless [is better] than many offspring, like [escaping] from a wolf. (Source untraced).
1,10: “Trembling, they have bellowed for the cool [water] that brings life.
(untraced) 1,10: *Śiśiram* means "cool"; it is derived from the root *śṛṇāti* ("to destroy") or *śamnāti* ("to pacify"). 1,10: “Release him toward this [Soma] when it is pressed. (RV 1,9,2)
1,10: He created him at the pressing;
"May our songs increase him" (ṚV V.21.92.21;
IX.61.14). 1,10: May our songs—our praises—increase him; for "songs" are so called from the root *gṛ* (to praise).
1,10: "This one indeed meets you" (ṚV 1,30,4). 1,10: This one meets you.
1,10: The particle *iva* is also seen here; it means "as if well-known" (*su-vidur-iva*) or "as if easily recognized" (*su-vijñāya-iva*).
1,10: Furthermore, *na* (not) is joined with *iti* (thus) in this way when expressing fear or danger (*paribhaya*).
1,11: "Some, with oblations, attend the celestial realms; others, pressing the Soma, [attend] at the libations" (RVKh 10.106.1).
1,11: "Rejoicing in our powers and in sacrificial gifts, may we not fall headlong into hell" (RVKh 10.106.1).

1,11: *Naraka* means hell; it is so called because there is no pleasure (*ramaṇa*) in that place, or because even the slightest [pleasure] does not exist therein. 1,11: Furthermore, the particle *na ca* is joined with this very word *iti* when used in response to a question, as in "And they do not drink *surā*.
1,11: *Surā* is derived from the root *su* (to press).
1,11: Thus they fall upon various high and low meanings; these are to be disregarded. 1,12:

Thus these four classes of words have been enumerated: nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles. 1,12: Among them, nouns are derived from verbs—so says Śākaṭāyana and the convention of the etymologists (nairukta).

1.12: "Not all [words]," says Gārgya; and some among the grammarians hold the same view. 1.12: In that case, where both accent and grammatical formation (*saṃskāra*) are capable [of conveying meaning] when accompanied by a local modification (*prādeśika-vikāra*—or *guṇa*, according to Bhartṛhari), those are recognized as such, just as in the cases of "cow," "horse," "man," and "elephant."

1.12: Now, if all nouns were derived from verbs, then whoever might perform that action, they would all have to be called by that [same] name. Furthermore, whoever might traverse a path, he too would have to be called "horse."

1.12: Whatever it might cut, even a blade of grass—that is what it is. Furthermore, if all nouns were derived from verbal roots, then a thing would receive its name only from as many [roots] as it is associated with.
1.12: In that case, there may be [names] such as Sthūṇā-dāra-śaya or Sañjanī.

1.13: Furthermore, whatever among these is a name derived from a rite (*kārmanāmika*) that is consistent with reason, and 1.13: moreover, they should pronounce them in such a way that their meanings are clearly understood.
1.13: They call the person dwelling in the city "puruṣa"; they call the horse "aṣṭā"; and they call grass "tardana.
Furthermore, even when the conventional usage is already established, they reflect upon it:
"Because of its spreading, they say 'pṛthivī' (the earth); who spread it out, and what was its support?"
1.13: Now, Śākaṭāyana [proposed] that when the meaning is not connected and no modification is prescribed, one should form new word-halves from the existing words.

He [prescribed] the causative suffix after the root *eti* (to go), as well as those beginning with the letter *y*; and after the root *asti* (to be), he [prescribed] the pure [root], as well as those beginning with the letter *s*. Furthermore, they say that "being" (*sattva*) precedes "becoming" (*bhāva*).
1,13: "The location of the prior [entity] cannot be established from the subsequent entity"—this is not tenable. 1,14:
For indeed, as it has been said:

1,14: When both accent and phonetic refinement are capable of being accompanied by a localized modification (or quality), then everything is considered localized; this being so, this objection does not hold. 1,14:
As for the statement that whatever action one might perform, they would designate all that substance accordingly—this is also addressed.
1.14: We observe that those who perform the same actions acquire the same name, while others do not. 1.14:

For instance, such as *takṣā* (carpenter), *parivrājaka* (wandering mendicant), *jīvana* (livelihood-earner), and *bhūmija* (earth-born); by this very [argument], the subsequent [objection] is answered. 1.14: As for the claim that "they should be explained in such a way that their meanings are well-known," there exist words that are rarely used even when they are primary derivatives (*aikapadika*), such as *vratati*, *damūnā*, *jāṭya*, *āṭṇāra*, *jāgarūka*, and *darvihomī*.
1,14: As for this [objection] that they deliberate upon speech once it has been completed—1,14: for indeed, when speech has been completed, there is an investigation into its application (yoga).
1,14: "The earth is so called because of its expansion," they say; but who expanded it, and what was its support?

1,14: Or rather, [the Veda] is broad by its very appearance, even if it has not been expanded by others; or else, all those who advocate for what has been seen [in the Veda] are equally subject to criticism.
As for the statement that he "collected the other half-words from the words," [this too is open to question].
1,14: He who applies a name to an object that lacks a corresponding reality is censurable for that reason; this is a censure of the person, not a censure of the scripture.

1,14: Regarding the claim that the designation of a prior entity by means of a subsequent entity is not tenable—we observe that certain previously arisen beings receive their names from subsequent entities, while others do not, as in the cases of "eater of bilva fruit" or "long-crested one."
1,14: [The word *bilva* is derived] either from the sense of "bearing" (*bharaṇa*) or from "splitting" (*bhedana*).
1,15: Furthermore, in the absence of this [knowledge], there is no comprehension of the meaning within the mantras.
For one who does not comprehend the meaning, the instruction regarding the phonetic refinement of accents cannot be fully accomplished.

1.15: This field of knowledge [grammar] is the completeness of grammar, which accomplishes its own purpose; and if it were useless for the comprehension of the meaning of the mantras, so says Kautsa, "for the mantras are indeed meaningless. This [objection] should be disregarded, because they possess fixed linguistic forms and a fixed sequence.
Furthermore, for a Brahmin, [the measures] endowed with form are prescribed:
with "Spread wide" (VS 1.22; TS I.8.1; VI.2.7.3; KS 1.8; 31.7;
MS I.9), he spreads [the altar]; with "I shall push forward," he pushes it forward.
Furthermore, there are [mantras] whose meanings are not logically applicable, such as:
"O herb, protect him! (TS I.2.1.1; III.5.1; VS III.3.2; KS II.1;
MS I.9.1) and "O axe, do not harm him! (VS IV.1; V.42; VI.15; TS I.2.1.1; III.5.1; VS III.3.2; KS II.1; MS II.1.1; ŚB IX.3.3)—so he says while [the priest] is actually performing the act of harming.
Furthermore, there are even contradictory statements:
"Rudra alone existed; there was no second," and "The Rudras upon the earth are innumerable thousands. (Vṣ. 16.54; ṃs. ī-9.9)
1,15: "O Indra, you were born without an enemy" (ṚV X,133,2;
SV 2,1152); 1,15: "Indra conquered a hundred armies at once" (ṚV X,103,1; SV 2,1199; Vṣ 17,33). Thus [it is said]. 1,15: Furthermore, he gives the command even to one who already knows.
1,15: "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni as he is being kindled. (TS 3.7.1; MS 1.4.11; TB 2.1.3.7.1; ŚB 5.2.9). Thus it is said. 1,15: Furthermore, it says that Aditi is everything:
"Aditi is heaven, Aditi is the intermediate space... (RV 1.89.10). Thus it is said.
1,15: We shall explain that further on.
1,15: Furthermore, there are [words] whose meanings are unclear, such as "amyak" (RV 1,169,3), "yādṛśmin" (RV 5,44,8), "jārayāyi" (RV 1,12,4), and "kāṇukā" (RV 2,1,77,4).
1.16: [The mantras] possess meaning, because they share the same nature as speech;

for the Brāhmaṇa states: "This indeed is the prosperity of the sacrifice—that which is perfect in form, when a mantra from the Ṛgveda or the Yajurveda speaks out while the ritual action is being performed" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 2.2.6); and also:
"Playing with sons and grandsons" (Ṛgveda X.85.42).
1,16: As for the claim that "formulations of fixed speech possess a fixed sequence," this is also the case among worldly expressions, such as "Indra and Agni" or "father and son. 1,16:

2,1: In those words where both accent and phonetic formation (*saṃskāra*) are capable of being endowed with a local modification (*prādeśika-vikāra*), one should explain them accordingly. 2,1:
But when the meaning is not [directly] connected and there is no local modification, one should examine the eternal meaning by means of some commonality of function (*vṛtti-sāmānya*).

2,1: Even when such a commonality does not exist, one should provide an etymological explanation based on commonalities of syllables or phonemes; however, one must never fail to provide an explanation.
2.1: One should not pay heed to grammatical refinement, for mental functions (vṛttayaḥ) are dependent upon objects.
2.1: One should apply case-endings according to the actual meaning. 2.1: In the case of verbal roots and so forth, only that which is offered and that which is taken out remain.

2,10: Their division [of the inheritance]. Regarding this, they relate an ancient history (*itihāsa*): Devāpi Ārṣṭiṣeṇa and Śāntanu, both Kauravyas, were brothers. 2,11: From the northern [ocean] the lower ocean is more elevated; the lower one is lower. 2,11:
"He does not run downward"—thus upward movement is prohibited.
2,11: The following [verse] is for the sake of providing a further etymological explanation of that.
2,12: "When Devāpi, the domestic priest of Śantanu, being chosen for the office of *hotṛ*, looked upon [the sacrifice] with compassion;
Bṛhaspati, hearing the gods and bestowing rain, granted him speech as a gift.
2,12: *Śantanu* means "may he be peaceful" (*śam tanotu*), or "may peace be extended to him" (*śam asmai tanv ā astu*).

2,12: The domestic priest places him at the front. Having been chosen for the office of the *hotṛ* priest, he meditated with longing: "May the gods hear me, O god-hearer; may they hear this one who desires the rain, who prays for rain. The gift was bestowed; the giver was Bṛhaspati, the Brahman. He offered speech to him. This is the extensive explanation of the *Bṛhat*. 2,13: The subsequent [verses] are common to both the Sky and the Sun.

2.13: However, those [names] which are its primary designations, we shall explain below. Why is he called Āditya? Because he takes up (ādatte) the essences; because he takes up the light among lights; because he is kindled with light; or because he is the son of Aditi. Yet, this usage of his is of little occurrence in the Vedic recensional texts (*ārca-abhyāmnāya*), as it appears only in the context of a specific hymn: "Sūrya, the son of Aditi, the son of Aditi."

2,13: In this same way, there are praises of other deities that proclaim them to be Ādityas, such as those of Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, Dakṣa, Bhaga, and Aṃśa. Furthermore, there are praises of Mitra and Varuṇa together: "O Ādityas, lords of liberal gifts" (dānunaspatī), meaning "lords of giving. Moreover, there is a Vedic verse concerning Mitra alone: "May the mortal who honors you with offerings, O Āditya, be preeminent through his observance of your law. Such is the Vedic testimony.
2,13: "Now, moreover, [we are under] the law of Varuṇa alone. "Now we, O Āditya, are in your *vratá*.

*Vratá* is a name for action, or it is so called because it restrains (*vārayati*) from non-performance; this other *vratá* is also so called because one chooses (*vṛṇoti*) it from that [restraint]. Food (*anna*) is also called *vratá*, because it covers (*āvṛṇoti*) the body. 2,14: *Svar* is the Āditya; he is *svar* because he moves well (*su-araṇaḥ*), he moves easily (*su-īraṇaḥ*), he is the essence of the true order (*su-ṛta-rasaḥ*), and he is the light of the luminaries of the true order (*su-ṛta-bhāḥ*). Or rather, *su-ṛta-bhāḥ* means "the speech of the true order" (*su-ṛta-bhāṣā*). By this, the heaven (*dyauḥ*) is also explained.

2,14: *Pṛśni* is the Āditya; the etymologists say it is so called because "it has partaken of color" (*varṇa*), being the toucher of flavors, the toucher of speech, and the light of the luminaries, or else it is that which is touched by speech.
2,14: The sky is touched by the luminaries and by those who perform meritorious deeds.
2,14: *Nāka* is the Āditya; he is the leader of the flavors, the leader of speech, and the leader of the luminaries.

2,14: Now, as for *dyauḥ* (the sky/heaven). *Kaṃ* is a name for happiness; that [happiness] which was established would here be negated: "Or rather, there is no heaven at all for one who has gone to that world.

2,14: Indeed, there is no heaven for one who has merely gone to that world; for only those who perform meritorious deeds go there. 2,14: The *go* (cow) is the sun; it causes the essences (*rasa*) to move, and they move within the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
2,14: Now, when the sky has gone far away from the earth, and when the luminaries depart from it;

2,14: the *vistap* becomes the sun (*āditya*), because it has entered (*ā-vista*) the essences, entered the speech of the luminaries, or entered the speech itself. 2,14: Then the sky is pervaded (*āvistā*) by the luminaries and by those who perform meritorious deeds.

2,14: *Nabhas* (the sky) becomes *āditya* (the sun), the leader of the fluids (*rasa*), the leader of the sounds (*bhāṣā*), or the guide of the lights (*jyotis*). Or rather, it may be the opposite of *bhanas* (shining); or it is so called because "it does not shine" (*na na bhāti*). By this, the heaven (*dyu*) is also explained. 2,15: The following fifteen words are names of rays (*raśmi*). A ray (*raśmi*) is so called because of its stretching (*yamanāt*). Of these, the first five are common to the rays of a horse. 2,15: The following eight words are names of the directions (*diś*).

2,15: Why "directions" (*diśaḥ*)? From the root *diś* [meaning] "to settle" (*āsadanāt*), or also from "to pervade" (*abhyaśanāt*). In that regard, the term "stages" (*kāsthāḥ*) is a name for many beings as well. The directions are "stages" (*kāsthāḥ*) because, having traversed them, they remain there.
2,15: The markers of the racecourse (*kāṣṭhā*) are so called because they stand having been stepped over one after another.
2,15: The sun is also called a *kāṣṭhā*, for it stands having traversed [its path]. 2,15: The finish line of a race is also called a *kāṣṭhā*, for it stands having been reached.

2,15: Even waters are called *kāṣṭhā*s, because they stand having traversed [their course]; thus [the term applies] to stationary things. 2,16: "In the midst of the standing, non-dwelling *kāṣṭhā*s, the body was placed;
the waters flow over Vṛtra’s secret place; Indra, his enemy, laid him in long darkness."
2,16: "Of those standing not [fixed]," that is, of those not settling down; [it refers to] the waters moving among unstable logs. "The body has been deposited"—this refers to the cloud. 2,16:
"Body" (*śarīra*) is derived from the root *śṛ* (to crush) or *śam* (to destroy).
2,16: "The waters move about and discern Vṛtra’s secret place of dissolution."

2,16: "Dīrgham" [is derived] from *drāghate* (he lengthens); "tamaḥ" from *tanoti* (he stretches). 2,16: "Āśayat" from *āśete* (he lies down). 2,16: "Indraśatruḥ"—Indra was his slayer (*śamayitā*), or he was the one who destroyed (*śātayitā*); therefore, he is called Indraśatru.

2,16: "Who is Vṛtra? The etymologists say he is a cloud; the historians say he is the Asura Tvaṣṭṛ. 2,16: "The act of raining arises from the process of mixing water and light; therein, descriptions of battle occur for the sake of metaphor. 2,16: "But indeed, the mantric verses and the discourses of the Brāhmaṇas [describe him] as being like a serpent."

2,16: [Vṛtra] obstructed the channels of the body as it was growing. When he was slain, the waters flowed forth; regarding this, there is this Ṛgvedic verse: 2,17: "The waters stood confined by Vṛtra, who had the Dāsas for his wives and the serpent for his guardian, like cows held back by the Paṇis.
That opening of the waters which had been covered, he opened up by slaying Vṛtra."

2,17: "The wives of Dāsa, the mistresses of Dāsa; *dāsa* comes from the root *das*, meaning he destroys the works [of others]. They stood with Ahi as their protector, guarded by Ahi. Ahi [comes] from *aya*, for he moves through the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). This other [serpent] also is called *ahi* for this very reason, though the prefix is shortened: it is called *ahi* because it strikes (*ahanti*). 'The waters were obstructed by Ahi, like cows [by a cowherd]. *Pani* means a merchant; *pani* comes from *panana* (praising/bartering). A merchant cleanses his wares (*panya*)."
2,17: "That which was the covered opening of the waters"—the *bila* (opening) is so called because it is a bearer (*bhara*), from the root *bhr* (to bear).

2,17: "Having slain Vṛtra, he opened [the waters]"—*Vṛtra* is so called from the root *vṛ* (to obstruct), or *vṛt* (to turn), or *vṛdh* (to grow). It is understood that his name *Vṛtra* derives from the fact that he obstructed (*avṛṇot*). 2,17: "Because he obstructed, that is the *vṛtratva* (nature of being Vṛtra) of Vṛtra"—so it is known.
2,17: "That which covered (avartata) is the etymological basis for Vṛtra's name," so it is known;
"that which grew (avardhata) is the etymological basis for Vṛtra's name," so it is known.
2,18: The following twenty-three [names] are synonyms for night.

2,18: Why "rātri" (night)? Because it causes those beings that roam by night to cease their activity; it causes others to cease [their activity] and makes them steady. Or, it may be from the root *rāti*, meaning "to give," for dewdrops are given forth (*pradīyante*) upon it. 2,18: The following sixteen are names of *uṣas* (dawn). 2,18: Why "uṣas"? Because she rises (*ucchati*), she is the truth.
2,18: The latter part of the night; regarding this, there is this [verse]:
2,19: "This best light among lights has come; a brilliant, far-reaching sign has been born.
Just as she was impelled for the impulse of Savitṛ, even so has Night yielded her womb to Uṣas."

2,19: "This has come, the best light among lights, wonderful, a brilliant sign; wisdom has been born, spreading abroad, dispelling the darkness. Just as Night, impelled by Savitṛ for the sake of his impulsion, yielded her womb and place to the Sun, even so did Night yield her womb and place to Dawn.
The female is the womb; the embryo has entered it. Regarding this, there is another verse: 2,19: "The female is the womb; the embryo has entered it.
Regarding this, there is another verse: [as follows].
2,20: "The bright one with the bright calf has come; she has left her dark dwelling places.
Of common kinship, immortal, following one after the other, the two move across the sky, changing their colors.
2,20: "With the bright calf" means having the sun as her calf; *ruśat* is a name for color, derived from the root *ruc*, meaning "to shine" or "to blaze."

2,20: He calls the sun her calf, either because of their constant companionship or because it carries away her essence (rasa). 2,20: "The bright one has come, shining white. *Śvetyā* [is derived from] the root *śvit*, meaning she has shone forth. *Kṛṣṇā* is the night; she is dark-colored for the sake of her dwelling. 2,20: *Kṛṣṇam* [is derived from] the root *kṛṣ*, meaning a low or inferior color.

2,20: Now he praises these two together: "Of common kin, of common bond, immortal, possessing the nature of immortality, following one after the other"—referring to each other—"[they] move through the space of heaven. These two are indeed the two heavens (*dyāvau*), because of their shining (*dyotana*).
Alternatively, it may mean "the two heavens move," that is, they move together with her. "Alternating, alternating" means making each other's inner self [manifest].

2,20: The following twelve are names of the day (*ahar*). Why "day" (*ahar*)? Because they bring their ritual acts (*karmāṇi*) toward it. This is its grammatical form (*nipāta*) in the verse addressed to Vaiśvānara.
2,21: "The black day and the white day revolve as two dust-clouds (*rajasī*) through the things to be known.
Vaiśvānara, like a king being born, has dispelled the darknesses with his light, Agni.

2,21: The black day is the night, and the white day is the day; these two dust-clouds revolve through the activities that are to be known. Like the sun rising as Vaiśvānara, the king of all lights, Agni has driven away the darknesses with his light.
2,21: Thirty subsequent names are for the cloud (*megha*).
2,21: Why "cloud" (*megha*)? Because it "moists" (*mehati*). 2,21: From the words *ā-upara* and *upala*, there are terms common with the names of mountains.

2,21: *Upara-upala* means "cloud," because the clouds rest (*uparamante*) upon it, or because they have come to rest (*uparatāḥ*) there; for these [clouds], this [verse] occurs: 2,22: "The first measures of the gods stood firm; from their cutting away, the clouds rose upward. Three heat the earth with moisture; two carry the swelling cloud."
2.22: Among the creations of the gods, the first ones stood forth; they were the central hosts of the gods.
"First" (*prathama*) is a name for the principal; he becomes the foremost.
He cut through the atmosphere, rending asunder the clouds.
2,22: From the cleaving of the clouds, water is produced.
2,22: Three heat the earth: Parjanya, Vāyu, and Āditya. By means of cold, heat, and rain, they ripen the plants; as "Anūpas," they cause the worlds to grow according to their respective functions.

2,22: This other [term] *anūpa* is derived from this very same root *anu-āp*, meaning "that which is reached by water," or it may be *anvāp* in the sense of "following after," just as in the case of *prāk*.
2,22: For that [word], *anūpa* would be used just as *prācīnam* is used.
2,22: [The verse says: "They carry the two-fold *bṛbūka* and the *purīṣa*."
2.22: Wind, the sun, and water.
2.22: *Bṛbūka* is a name for water; it is derived either from the root *brū*, meaning "to speak," or from *bhraṃś*, meaning "to fall.
2.22: *Purīṣa* is derived from the root *pṛṇ*, meaning "to satisfy," or from *pṛ*, meaning "to fill."

2.23: Hereafter follow fifty-seven names of Vāc. Why is she called Vāc? Because she speaks (*vac*). Regarding her, there are Vedic citations (*nigama*) for Sarasvatī that apply both to a river and to a deity. Of these, those concerning the deity we shall explain later.

2,23: Now this is like a river. 2,24: "This one, with her surging waves, has broken through the ridges of the mountains like a lotus-root-digger; with her powerful billows, we would serve Sarasvatī—the slayer of Pārāvata—with well-fashioned hymns and inspired thoughts for our protection."

2,24: *iyam* (this); *śusmaiḥ* (with dryings); *śosanaiḥ* (with desiccations); *śuṣmam*—this is a name for strength (*bala*), because it causes one to wither (*śosayati*). 2,24: *bisam* (lotus root); from the root *biṣ*, which signifies the action of splitting (*bhedana*) or the action of increasing (*vṛddhi*).
2,24: *sānu* (ridge); it is that which is raised up (*samucchritam*) or that which has been elevated (*samunnunnam*).
2,24: With great waves;

[we worship] Sarasvatī, the river that slays the *pārāvata* (the one who stays on the far shore), who destroys both the far and the near shores—the far shore being that which is supreme and the near shore being that which is inferior—for the sake of protection, with well-fashioned hymns, that is, with beautiful praises and ritual acts.
2,24: Hereafter follow one hundred and one names for water.
2,24: Why "water" (*udaka*)? Because it moistens (*unatti*) that which exists.
2,24: The following thirty-seven [names] are names of rivers (*nadī*). 2,24: Why "river" (*nadī*)? Because these roar (*nadanā*); they possess sound.
2,24: Among these, the *naighaṇṭuka* usage is frequent and wonderful, as it were, primarily.
2,24: Regarding this, they relate a traditional history (*itihāsa*): the seer Viśvāmitra was the domestic priest (*purohita*) of Sudās Paijavana.

2,24: Viśvāmitra means "friend of all" or "all-encompassing"; Sudās means "giving auspicious gifts"; Paijavana is the son of Pijavana; and Pijavana, moreover, means either "possessing enviable speed" or "one whose movement is unmixed."
2.24: Having taken his leave, he went to the confluence of the Vipāś and Śutudrī, and the others followed him.

Viśvāmitra praised the rivers, saying, "Become fordable," both in the dual and in the plural; we shall explain later that which is in the dual, and now this which is in the plural: 2.25: "O you who follow the *ṛta*, rest for a moment at my Soma-like speech, by means of these [verses]."
2,25: Seeking aid, the son of Kuśika has called out with lofty wisdom toward the Sindhu river.
2,25: "Cease [your flow] for my Soma-like speech, O you who provide the Soma, O you who possess the cosmic order (*ṛta*)!
2,25: *Ṛta* is a name for water; thus it becomes the response to *ṛta*."
2,25: [It is measured] by moments (*muhūrta*), by solar courses (*ayana*), or by seasons (*ayana*).

2,25: A *muhūrta* is "a moment" (*muhur*) of a season (*ṛtu*); a season is so called from the root *ṛ*, meaning "to go" or "motion. Time is called *muhūrta* because it is, as it were, momentarily bewildered (*mūdha*), and because it occurs repeatedly (*abhīkṣṇam*). 2,25: It becomes *abhīkṣṇam* (repeatedly) from *abhikṣanam*; a *kṣaṇa* (moment) is derived from the root *kṣan*, meaning "to cut," for time is something that cuts away.
2,25: *Kālaḥ* [is derived] from the root *kal*, which has "motion" as its object.

2,25: "I invoke the Sindhu with a great hymn (*bṛhatyā*), with a lofty mind (*mahatyā manīṣayā*)—that is, with a mental impulse (*manasa īṣayā*), or with praise (*stuti*), or with wisdom (*prajñā*)—for the protection (*avanāya*) of Kuśika’s son.

2,25: "Kuśika was a king; [the name is derived] from the root *kruś*, which has 'sound' as its object, or perhaps from *kraṃś*, which has 'making manifest' as its object, meaning 'one who clearly proclaims' (*sādhu vikrośayitā*) matters."
2.25: The rivers replied: 2.26: "Indra, whose arm wields the thunderbolt, dug us out; he struck down Vṛtra, the enclosure of the rivers.
The god Savitṛ, the skillful-handed, led us forth; by his impulse we flow wide."
2,26: Indra, whose arm wields the thunderbolt, has carved us out; *radati* means he digs, performing his work. 2,26: "He struck down Vṛtra, the enclosure of the rivers"—this has been explained.
2,26: The god Savitṛ, the one with beautiful hands, the one with auspicious hands, has led us.

2,26: *Pāṇi* is derived from the root *pan*, which has the sense of "to honor"; having taken hold of the *pāṇis*, they honor the gods. 2,26: "In its impulsion (*prasava*), we go forth, wide-stretching.
2,26: *Urvīḥ* is derived from the roots *ūrṇoti* ("to cover") or *vṛṇoti* ("to choose"), according to Aurnavābha.
2,26: Having rejected [the offerings], they finally heard [him].
2,27: "We shall hear your words, O Kārava; you have come from afar with wagon and chariot.
We bow down before you like a swelling woman; we wait upon you constantly like a maiden for her suitor."
2,27: We have heard your commands, O Kāru; come from afar with wagon and chariot. We bend down to you as a woman nursing her son, or as a maiden bends down to embrace her lover—or so it is said.
2,27: The following twenty-six verses are names of horses.
2,27: Of these, the last eight are in the plural.
2,27: Why "aśva"? Because it traverses the path (*adhvan*), or because it is a great eater (*mahā-aśana*).

Regarding that, the term *dadhikrā* means either "he who strides while bestowing" (*dadhat krāmati*), or "he who cries out while bestowing" (*dadhat krandati*), or "he who becomes one who utters the sound 'ā' while bestowing" (*dadhat ākārī bhavati*).
Its Vedic citations (*nigama*) pertain both to the horse and to the deity.
2,27: That which is "possessing deities" (*devatāvat*) we shall explain later; now this [section] is "possessing horses" (*aśvavat*).
2,28: "And his vigorous steed, bound at the neck, between the flanks, and in the mouth, speeds toward the swift course.
Dadhikrā, having celebrated his resolve, leaps along the curves of the paths."

2,28: Furthermore, *api* means "possessing speed" (*vājī*); being impetuous, he swiftly traverses the path along his gallop. *Grīvā* is so called because it is bound (*badh-*) to the neck, or from the root *gṛ* (to swallow), or *gṛ* (to praise), or *gṛ* (to seize). *Apikakṣa* and *āsani* have been explained [in the preceding commentary]. 2,28: *Dadhikrāḥ*, having repeatedly exerted himself (*anu-saṃ-tavītvat*), applies his will (*kratu*)—that is, either action (*karman*) or wisdom (*prajñā*).
2,28: This is a Vedic citation (*nigama*) with the preceding verbal root *tan* (to extend) as its base form.
2,28: *Pathām* refers to the bends of paths; *pathām* refers to their curves. *Panthāḥ* is derived from the root *pat* (to fall), or *pad* (to go), or *panth* (to go).
2,28: *Aṅkaḥ* is derived from the root *añc* (to bend); it is formed with the suffix *āpanīphnat*, which is a reduplicated (*carkarīta*) formation of the root *phan*.
2,28: They say that ten subsequent [sections] are "designations" (*ādista*) for practical application, intended for the sake of understanding through association.
2.28: There are eleven verbal roots (dhātus) beginning with *jvalati*. 2.28: There are exactly as many subsequent names for those that shine (*jvalataḥ*).
3.1: There are twenty-six subsequent names of actions (*karma-nāmāni*).
3,1: Action (karman). Why? Because it is performed (*kriyate*) by one who exists (*sataḥ*). 3,1: The following fifteen [terms] are names of offspring (*apatya*).
3,1: Offspring (*apatya*). Why? Because it does not fall away (*na apatatam bhavati*), or because it does not cause one to fall (*na anena patati*).

3,1: Just as offspring are produced by a progenitor, so shall we cite examples from the *ṛc*s concerning wealth (*arthīya*). 3,2: "For the wealth of the stranger is to be shared; may we be masters of eternal riches. O Agni, there is no offspring of another that remains [for us]; do not lead us astray from the path of the mindless."
For one must avoid, not approach, the wealth of the stranger; the stranger remains one who does not cross over.
"Wealth" (*rekna*) is a name for riches, for it is what is left over when given away. May we be masters of eternal wealth, as if of ancestral property.

3,2: There is no offspring other than the fire (*agni*). "Offspring" (*śeṣa*) is a name for progeny; it remains (*śiṣyate*) for one who is striving, yet it belongs to one who is heedless and lacks awareness. [The verse] "May they not abandon us from the path" is followed by the next [verse] for the sake of further etymological explanation:
3,3: "For no stranger, however kind, can be grasped as one's own; nor can a brother born of another womb be so considered in the mind."
3,3: "Then indeed, that horse returns again to its own dwelling; may the vigorous steed come toward us anew. [249] 3,3:

"For he is not to be grasped, nor is he a stranger, though he be the most beloved even as one's own uterine brother; he is not to be thought of by the mind even as 'this is my son. [249] 3,3: "And then he goes back again to that very dwelling from which he came. [249]
3,3: "Okas" is said to be a name for a dwelling place.
3,3: "May the vigorous one, the impeller, who overcomes his rivals, come to us—he who is newly born, he indeed is the son.
3,3: Now, they cite this [verse] regarding the inheritance of a daughter.

3,4: "The wise priest, instructing and honoring the ordinance of *ṛta*, went toward the granddaughter of his daughter; there the father, performing the seminal flow of his daughter, hastened with a favorable mind. [250] 3,4: The one who knows impels the daughter toward the state of being a son for the purpose of establishing continuity. [250]

3,4: [She is called] *duhitā* because she is ill-disposed (*durhitā*), or because she is placed far away (*dūre hitā*), or because she milks out (*dogdheḥ*). 3,4: He approached his grandson, the son of his daughter, the son of his son. 3,4: Being wise, he honored the ordinance of the sacrifice of procreation—that which has arisen from every limb, born from the heart, and produced by the mother 5,5: The chest has been explained.

well-stepping, easy to step upon.

5.7: "Śipiviṣṭa" and "Viṣṇu"—these are two names of Viṣṇu.

"Powerful" (*tavasa*) is a name for the Great One; he has arisen, dwelling in the far distance of this space, in the transcendent realm. 5.9: "The glowing one" (*āghṛṇiḥ*); "glowing" (*āgata-hṛṇiḥ*).
5,9: "O glowing one, let us associate. Come, O wrathful one, let us serve together.

With the movement of the hands—that is, by the motion of the hands—they have generated the praiseworthy one, the far-seeing master of the house, who is never weary. 5,11: "With a single draught he drank up three hundred lakes at once—Indra, in his longing for Soma."

5,11: *Ekena pratidhānena apibat* means "he drank together at once. 5,11: *Indraḥ somasya kānukā*: [the word] *kānukā* means "desirable things" (*kāntakāni*), or "things traversed" (*krāntakāni*), or "things made" (*kṛtakāni*); or it means "Indra is the desirer of the Soma," or [it refers to] *kāne ghātaḥ*, or *kāne hataḥ*, or "struck by desire" (*kānti-hataḥ*). 5,11: Regarding this, the ritualists inform us that there are thirty *uktha*-cups at the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*) dedicated to a single deity; they drink from them at this time with a single pouring-in (*pratidhāna*), and these are called *saras*.

5,11: "The etymologists [say] there are thirty days and nights of the waning fortnight and thirty of the waxing fortnight. Those rays which are the waters belonging to the moon that are about to come, they drink them during the waning fortnight;

thus also there is a Vedic verse: 'Whom the imperishable ones drink as the imperishable. During the waxing fortnight, they cause him to swell; thus also there is a Vedic verse: 'Just as the gods cause the stalk to swell.'"

5,11: The *adhṛgu* mantra occurs because [the priest] is authorized over the cow; or rather, it may be intended as a command, because it possesses that specific word: "O *adhṛgu*, perform the service! Perform the service well! Perform the service, O *adhṛgu*! 5,11: Agni is also called *adhṛgu*:
"For you, O *adhṛgu*, the powerful [oblations] drip."
5.11: [The word *adhrigu*] possesses the activity of unrestrained movement.

5,11: The *āṅgūṣa* is the resonance of the *stoma*.

"Āpāntamanyu, whose onset is fierce, the shaker, the powerful, the arrow-bearer, the straight-rushing."

[He is] the one whose abode is strength, the one who flies with strength.

(VS 3.48). 5.18: Thus there is also a scriptural citation.

5,21: A wolf saw the host of stars traveling along its path; having observed them, it springs upon them one by one, according to which the moon is about to yoke itself.
Like a carpenter working on a back ailment, [it fashions them].
5,21: "O Heaven and Earth, know this of me.

5.27: You are *sudeva*, O Varuṇa—you are a beautiful god (*kalyāṇadeva*) or a desirable god (*kāmanīyadeva*). To you belong the seven rivers; from your flowing comes the river, for your seven streams flow along your palate (*kākuda*), just as they flow along the hollow of a beautiful-waved vessel. 5.27: *Bīriṭam* is the atmosphere; thus said Ṛīki. It is so called because it is prior to the act of weaving (*vayati*) and subsequent to the act of moving (*irati*), or because the rays (*vayāṃsi*) rest within it, or because the lights (*bhāṃsi*) rest within it. 5.27: Regarding this, they cite this verse; there is also a Vedic usage (*nigama*) [to support it].
5,28: "The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) of these [gods] has been well-spread; like two lords of the people (*viśpati*), they come with vigor.

(ṚV 7,39,2) 5,28: The sacrificial grass of these [gods] is spread out, providing a good path for their approach. They come as the protectors or guardians of all.

"Ni-yut-vān" means he whose horses are the *niyuts*.

5.28: Śākapūṇi says it means "to reach" (*acchābher āptum*). 5.28: [The forms] *parīmaḥ* and *sīmaḥ* have already been explained.
5.28: This [verse] is explained by the same [method as] *enam*, *enām*, *asyai*, and *asya*.

6,1: *Śuk* is from the root *śocate*.

6,1: *Śuciḥ* (the pure). It is derived from the root *śuc*, meaning "to shine" or "to blaze. 6,1: This other [meaning of] *śuci* is also derived from this very same root.

6,1: They are called *āśā* because they sit (*āsadanāt*) [therein]; they are called *upadiś* because they are seen from nearby (*abhy-aśanāt*).

6,1: A *kāśi* is a handful; it is a *muṣṭi* because of its manifestation (*prakāśanāt*), or because of its grasping (*mocanāt*), or because of its seizing (*moṣaṇāt*), or because of its deluding (*mohanāt*).

6,1: "O Indra, even these two boundless worlds, whatever you grasp, O Maghavan, they are yours. 6,1: These two, Indra, the *rodasī*, the two banks—*dyāvāpṛthivī* (heaven and earth)—are so called because of obstructing (*virodhanāt*). A bank (*rodhaḥ*) is that which obstructs; it holds back the current, like a shore.
It is derived from the root *rujati* (to break), in its reverse sense; whereas a clod of earth (*loṣṭaḥ*) is not in the reverse sense. [They are] boundless, at the far limit.
6,1: O Maghavan, that which you grasp is your great power. 6,1: "O Indra, you crushed the handless Kuṇāru.
6,1: Having rendered him handless, O Indra, you crushed the thundering cloud.

6,2: "O Indra, the cloud *vala*—the piercer (*alātṛṇaḥ*)—having been afraid before the slaying of the cow-pen (*go-vraja*), opened it wide. He made the paths easy to traverse for the cows to go forth; the voices, blowing [in praise], helped the one invoked by many. (ṚV 3,30,10) 6,2: *Alātṛṇaḥ* means "sufficiently piercing"; *vala* is so called from the root *vṛ*, meaning "to cover"; *vraja* is so called because it moves within the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Before the slaying of this cow—the speech belonging to the intermediate region (*mādhyamikā vāk*)—it was afraid and opened wide.
6,2: He made the paths easy to traverse for the release of the cattle;
he made the paths easy to travel for the emergence of the cows. The sounding voices have favored the one invoked by many.
6,2: [The word] *āpaḥ* is derived from "flowing" (*ā-vahana*) or from "speaking" (*vāc-vadana*).
When many [people] call out, it becomes water; the root *dhamati* has the sense of motion. 6,3:
"Uproot the *rakṣas*, O Indra, together with its root; cut off its middle; crush what is fresh!"
"6,3: How far have you pursued the *salalūka*? You have cast your burning heat upon the hater of sacred knowledge (*brahmadviṣ*). (ṚV 3.30.17) 6,3: Uproot the *rakṣas*, O Indra, along with its root!
6,3: The word 'root' (*mūla*) is so called because of its being uprooted (*mocana*), or because of its being destroyed (*moṣaṇa*), or because of its being deluded (*mohana*)."
6.3: "Cut the middle; crush the tip.
From what extent does it become "arrived at the tip"?
It becomes "salalūka," meaning "greedy" or "evil," according to the etymologists (nairuktāḥ).

*Bhārjīkaḥ* means one whose light is well-known.

(RV 9.112.3). 6,6: "I am a poet, a maker of hymns, and then a physician."

*Jigarti* means "one who swallows" (*girati*), or "one whose action is swallowing" (*giraṇa-karman*), or "one whose action is praising" (*gṛṇāti-karman*), or "one whose action is seizing" (*gṛhṇāti-karman*).
"O wise one, like a hero, we do not [know] your greatness; O Agni, you alone truly know it."

"For I have heard that you two are the greatest givers of much, whether from a father-in-law or even from a brother-in-law.
Therefore, O Indra and Agni, as the Soma is being offered to you, I generate a new hymn of praise" (Ṛgveda 1.109.2).
6,9: For I have heard that you two are more generous givers than even a son-in-law who is not well-acquainted with his father-in-law’s sister.
6,9: "Son-in-law" (vijāmātṛ)—so the people of the South constantly call a purchased husband, as if he were an unwanted suitor.
6,9: A son-in-law (jāmātṛ) is one who produces offspring; he is either the maker of that [offspring] or perhaps even from a brother-in-law (syāla).

6.9: "He is near his brother-in-law (*syāla*) by virtue of their connection," so say the Naidānas. Or rather: "He scatters the parched grains (*lāja*). Regarding *lāja*, it is derived from the root *lāj*; *syam* refers to the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), which is derived from the root *śyā*. A winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) is so called because it winnows (*sūryati*) food; or alternatively, it is derived from the root *śṛ* (to crush).
6,9: Now, through the offering of Soma, O Indra and Agni, I generate for you two a new, ever-fresh hymn of praise.

"O Indra and Soma, let the one who utters evil and intends harm be scorched, like a cauldron placed over fire."

O Aśvins, you raised up Atri, who had been cast down into the pit, together with his entire retinue, for his well-being.

(ṚV 1.116.8) By means of cold water at the end of summer, you two warded off the scorching heat of Agni; you bestowed upon him, for the sake of Aṅga, that nourishing strength which sustains life. That Agni who was in the *ṛbīsa*—that is, within the earth, within plants and trees, and within the waters—you two raised him up, together with his entire retinue and all his names.

6.36: *Gaṇa* [is so called] because it is a collection (*gaṇanāt*) and because it possesses qualities (*guṇa*). 6.36: That the plants arise when it rains and that living beings on earth flourish—that is the form of the Aśvins; with that he praises them, he praises them.
7.1: [Now begins the section on deities. Om! Now, therefore, the section on deities.]
7.1: Those names which belong to deities praised for their preeminence, they call "having that as its deity" (*tad-daivata*). This is the examination of this deity.
Whatever desire a seer has, and toward whichever deity he applies a hymn of praise while seeking lordship over that [object], that mantra becomes one whose deity is that [deity].

7,1: Furthermore, this praise (*stuti*) is fourfold: by name (*nāman*), by kinship (*bandhu*), by action (*karman*), and by form (*rūpa*). It has been stated that praise consists of name, form, action, and kinship (*Durga*, p. 717; cf. *Bṛhaddevatā* 1.7). 7,1: Those *ṛc* verses are of three kinds: those composed in the indirect mode (*parokṣakṛta*), those composed in the direct mode (*pratyakṣakṛta*), and those concerning the self (*ādhyātmikī*). 7,1: Among these, those composed in the indirect mode are joined with all nominal case-endings (*nāmavibhakti*) and with the third person (*prathamapuruṣa*) verbal endings.

7,2: "Indra rules over heaven; Indra rules over the earth. "To Indra indeed [sing] the singers the lofty [song]. "By Indra these Tṛtsus, striving together... "Sing the Sāman for Indra. "Without Indra, no domain whatsoever flows pure. "I shall proclaim now the heroic deeds of Indra. "In Indra desires have been gathered. [717]

7,2: Now, there are forms of address in the middle voice directed toward the person present, such as "you" (*tvam*) and other personal names—for example: "O Indra, [come] from beyond strength," and "O Indra, strike away our enemies. [718]
