For example: "Indra Vaikuṇṭha," "The Lava-hymn," and "Vāc Āmbhṛṇīyā. 7.3:
Mantras composed in the third person (*parokṣa-kṛta*) and those composed in the first person (*pratyakṣa-kṛta*) are the majority; those concerning the self (*ādhyātmika*) are few.
7,3: Furthermore, it is indeed a hymn of praise (*stuti*) and not a declaration of a benediction (*āśis-vāda*), as in this hymn: "Now I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Indra.
[725] 7,3: [ḍ.p.726: In that case, however, a benediction should be applied.
7,3: For what reason?

7,3: For praise is employed for the sake of a prayer (*āśis*). 7,3: Moreover, there are cases where it is a prayer alone and not praise, such as: "May I be well-eyed with my eyes; may I be full of splendor with my face; may I be well-hearing with my ears. 7,3: This [usage] is frequent in the *Ādhvaryava* [Veda] and in sacrificial mantras. [In those instances as well, praise must be applied; for a deity that is not praised does not fulfill the prayer.]
7,3: Furthermore, there are oaths and curses: "May I die this very day if I am a sorcerer," and "Then may he be deprived of his ten sons.
[725] 7,3: Furthermore, there is the desire to declare a certain state of being: "Death was not, nor was there immortality then," and "In the beginning, darkness was hidden by darkness. [725]

7,3: Furthermore, lamentation (*paridevanā*) arises from some state of being, as in: "A good god shall fly away today, never to return," and "I do not know whether I exist or not. [725] Thus, this wailing preceded by self-reproach is called lamentation.
7,3: Furthermore, it consists of blame and praise, as in: "He who eats alone becomes solely sinful," and "This house of Bhoja is like a lotus pond.
[725] Likewise, in the *Akṣasūkta*, there is both the blame of gambling and the praise of agriculture. [726]

7,3: Thus, the seers’ visions of mantras arise through various high and low intentions. [726] Regarding that, both the *nidāna* (origin stories) and the *ārṣa-anukramaṇī* (succession lists of seers) should be consulted.
[733] 7,4: Therefore, regarding those mantras whose deities have not been specified, an investigation into the deity must be conducted. [733]

7,4: Whatever deity a sacrifice or a sacrificial limb belongs to, those [limbs] have that as their deity. [733] (For this is the principle: "In cases where the deity is doubtful, the determination of the deity follows from the context. That which is employed at the morning pressing belongs to Agni; that which is at the midday pressing belongs to Indra; that which is at the third pressing belongs to Āditya. [734]) 7,4: Now, regarding those other than the sacrifice, the ritualists say they belong to Prajāpati, while the etymologists say they belong to Nārāśaṃsa. 7,4: [Regarding the statement: "The sacrifice, says Kātyakya; Agni, says Śākapūṇi."

7,4: By the word *yajña* (sacrifice), Viṣṇu is also expressed; for it is known from scripture: "Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice. And since it is known that "Agni is the deity who receives the greatest share among the deities," therefore a mantra whose indicative mark (*liṅga*) does not manifest a specific deity should be addressed to Agni.
7,4: Furthermore, because he is the locus of all deities, it is known from scripture: "Agni is indeed all the deities; in him, indeed, all the deities abide. 7,4:
Some, however, observing that a mantra by which men are praised is a *nārāśaṃsa*, consider it to be a hymn of praise to human beings.

7,4: That is incorrect; for praise by means of mantras whose gender is not manifest is not appropriate for human beings, because those [mantras] are difficult to understand and because humans possess limited intelligence.
7,4: Or rather, that [deity] may be a deity according to one's desire; for, according to one's wish—that is, by choice—one should conceive of a deity in that [mantra].

7,4: [The section on *prāya* (D.736)] Or it refers to the deity; or rather, it signifies abundance (D.736). For there is a common practice in the world of abundance: "O God of Gods" is used for that which has the guest as its deity, or that which has the ancestors as its deity. When it is thus specified, whatever remains from that collection belongs in common to the gods, the ancestors, and humans (p.737). [733] 7,4: A mantra is either sacrificial (*yājña*) or divine (*daivata*). [733] 7,4: That mantra whose indicative mark of a deity is not manifest is either sacrificial or divine. It is known from scripture: "Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice."

7,4: Furthermore, according to the etymologists (*nairuktāḥ*), Viṣṇu is indeed Āditya himself, because he is recorded as being in the same position as *dyu* (the sky/heaven); for it will be stated [later]: "Whatever is mysterious (*pravalhitam*) is indeed the work of Āditya.
Therefore, that mantra must have Āditya as its deity.

7,4: Alternatively, that mantra is "daivata" (pertaining to a deity). It is called *daivata* because the deity is contained within it (*asmin devatā*). For the quality of being the deity belongs primarily to Agni alone, since he encompasses all deities; as it is known from scripture: "Agni, indeed, is all the deities," and "Agni, indeed, receives the greatest share among the deities. Furthermore, according to the principle that "what is not specifically assigned [to another] goes to the principal," that mantra must therefore belong to Agni.

7,4: Regarding that which was stated by way of introduction—"The Nairuktas say they are the *nārāśaṃsa*s"—that very point has been determined according to the opinion of Kātyāyana and Śākapūṇi as being "the sacrifice or Agni," for those two are indeed Nairuktas. [Ḍ. 737–738] 7,4:

For even non-deities are praised as if they were deities, such as those beginning with the horse and ending with plants; furthermore, there are eight pairs. 7,4: One should not consider these to be adventitious attributes of the deities, for this is something directly perceived.
7,4: Due to the great majesty of the deity, the single Self is praised in many ways; other deities become the various limbs of that one Self.
Furthermore, they say that the seers praise [the deity] according to the diverse natures of beings, because of the universal name of "nature" (*prakṛti*).
They are born from one another.
7,4: They have various natures; they are born of action; they are born of the self. For them, the self alone becomes the chariot, the self the horses, the self the weapon, and the self the arrow.
7,4: "The self is everything of every god. [723–724] 7,5:

"There are only three deities," say the etymologists (nairukta): Agni, whose station is the earth; Vāyu, or Indra, whose station is the intermediate space; and Sūrya, whose station is the sky. [745] 7,5: Due to their great majesty, even for each single one of them there are many names.
7,5: Or rather, because the actions are distinct, it is as in the case of one person who is [designated] as the Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, Brahman, and Udgātṛ.
7,5: Or rather, they should indeed be separate, for the praises are separate, and likewise the designations.
7,5: As for this [argument] that "because the actions are distinct," even many [priests] may perform the actions by dividing them [among themselves].
7,5: In that regard, the unity of configuration and the unity of enjoyment are to be disregarded.
7,5: Just as on earth, humans, cattle, and gods are seen to have a unity of place and a unity of enjoyment.
7,5: Just as the earth [is shared] with the rain-cloud, and with wind and the sun, and there is enjoyment with fire for the rest of the world; in that case, this is like a human chariot.
7,6: Now, the contemplation of the forms of the deities.
One view is that they should be anthropomorphic, for their praises and designations are like those of sentient beings.
Another reason is that they are praised with limbs having human form, as in: "O Indra, the arms of you, the ancient one," and "When you grasp it, O Maghavan, what was your intention? [754]

7,6: Furthermore, by means of *puruṣavidhika* substances and combinations [such as]: "O Indra, come with your two bay horses (*haribhyām*)," and "A beautiful wife is in your house, O god. 7,6: Furthermore, by means of *puruṣavidhika* ritual acts.
7,6: "Eat, O Indra, and drink of that which has been set forth.
7,6: "O you whose ears hear, listen to our call. 7,6/[755] 7,7: "They may be of non-human form," so it is another [view]. 7,6/[761]
7,7: Furthermore, that which is seen to be non-human in form is, for example, fire, wind, the sun, the earth, and the moon.
[761] 7,7: As for the statement that "praises are indeed like those of sentient beings," even insentient things are praised in this way, such as everything from dice up to medicinal herbs.
[761] 7,7: As for the statement that "they are praised by means of limbs possessing human characteristics," this also applies to insentient objects.
7,7: “They cry out with the golden oxen”—this is a praise of the pressing-stones (*grāva-stuti*).

As for that which [is expressed] by means of substances associated with human activities, that too is of the same nature; “The Sindhu has harnessed the easy chariot drawn by horses”—this is a praise of the river (*nadī-stuti*). As for that which [is expressed] by means of actions associated with human activities, that too is of the same nature; “Even before the Hotṛ, they have eaten the sacrificial oblation”—this is indeed a praise of the pressing-stones.

7.7: Or rather, they may be of both kinds. Or again, even while being non-human in form, these may have action as their essence, just as the sacrifice is the essence of the sacrificer; this is the established convention regarding narrative accounts.

7.8: It was stated previously that there are only three deities; we shall now explain their association with specific portions [of the Veda]. [This association with portions is stated so that, when a mantra contains a word whose deity is not explicitly known, the deity may be understood through such association with a portion.]

7,8: Now, these are the portions belonging to Agni: this world, the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), spring, the *gāyatrī* metre, the *trivṛt* stoma, the *rathantara* sāman, and those groups of deities recited in the first position. [765] 7,8: Agnāyī, Pṛthivī, and Īḷā are the females. [765] 7,8: Furthermore, his function consists of the carrying of the oblations, the summoning of the deities, and whatever else pertains to the domain of sacrificial offerings; all that is indeed the work of Agni. [766] (By association with him, even when the word "Agni" is not explicitly present, the mantra becomes one dedicated to Agni. [766]
7,8: Now, his deities with whom he is praised [as Agni is praised together with them; for example, Ḍ 767] are Indra, Soma, Varuṇa, Parjanya, the Seasons, and the oblation for Agni and Viṣṇu [765].
7,8: However, no verse containing such praise is found among the Daśatayīs [the ten Maṇḍalas of the Ṛgveda].

7,8: Furthermore, there is the oblation for Agni and Pūṣan, but there is no praise [for them together]; in that regard, they cite this verse as an instance of praise through grammatical case-forms (vibhakti-stuti). [765]
7,9: "May Pūṣan, the wise one, whose cattle are never lost, the guardian of the world, move you from here.
May he entrust you to these fathers, and may Agni deliver you to the benevolent gods.
[770] "Pūṣan, the wise one, whose cattle are never lost, the guardian of the world"—for this Āditya is indeed the protector of all beings. [770]
7,9: "He hands you over to these fathers"—this third quarter-verse is subject to doubt.
7,9: One view is that *pūṣan* is mentioned first as a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), while another is that *agni* is mentioned last as a formal proclamation (*prakīrtana*).

7,9: Regarding the phrase "Agni for the gods who are easy to find" (*suvidatriyebhyaḥ*), "easy to find" (*suvidatra*) refers to wealth; it may derive from the root *vid* with the prefix *su*, or it may derive from the root *dā* with the two prefixes *su* and *vi*.

7,10: Now, these are the portions belonging to Indra: the intermediate world (*antarikṣa-loka*), the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*), summer (*grīṣma*), the *triṣṭubh* meter, the fifteenfold hymn-form (*pañcadaśa-stoma*), the *bṛhat* sāman, and those hosts of gods who are enumerated as belonging to the middle station, as well as women.
7,10: Furthermore, his function is the bestowing of sap and the slaying of Vṛtra. Whatever action is performed with power, that indeed is the work of Indra. [772]
7,10: Now, his associated deities are Agni, Soma, Varuṇa, Pūṣan, Bṛhaspati, Brahmanaspati, Parvata, Kutsa, Viṣṇu, and Vāyu.
Furthermore, Mitra is praised together with Varuṇa; Soma with Rudra; Pūṣan with Agni; and Parjanya with Vāta. 7,11:
Now, these are the divisions belonging to the Ādityas.

7,11: That world; the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*); the rainy season; the *jagatī* metre; the seventeenfold hymn-form (*saptadaśastoma*); the *vairūpa* chant; and those hosts of gods enumerated in the highest station, beginning with the Ādityas, as well as the women.
7,11: Now, its function is the drawing up of essence by means of its rays and the sustaining of that essence; whatever is impelled is indeed the work of the Sun. 7,11:
There is praise [of it] by means of the Moon, the Wind, and the Year.
7,11: Within these very arrangements of positions (*sthānavyūha*), one should determine the remaining distribution (*bhaktiśeṣa*) of the *ṛtu*, *chandas*, *stoma*, and *pṛṣṭha* [elements].

7,11: "The autumn, the *anuṣṭubh* metre, the twenty-one-fold *stoma*, and the *vairāja* sāman—these have the earth as their abode. 7,11: "The winter, the *paṅkti* metre, the twenty-seven-fold *stoma*, and the *śākvara* sāman—these have the intermediate space as their abode. [Note: Even if a mantra lacks a characteristic mark of Agni (*anagniliṅga*), if it contains any one of these [elements], it should be understood as being addressed to Agni. Cf. KB 23.5.37.
7.11: "The cold season (*śiśira*), the *aticchandas* metre, the thirty-threefold hymn-form (*trayastriṃśa-stoma*), and the *raivata* chant—these are the portions belonging to the day.
7.12: "Mantras are so called because they are for the purpose of reflection (*manana*). 7.12: "Metres (*chandāṃsi*) are so called because they provide concealment or protection (*chādana*)."
7.12: *Stoma* is derived from the root *stu* (to praise). 7.12: *Yajus* is derived from the root *yaj* (to sacrifice).
7.12: *Sāman* is that which is measured by the *ṛc*; or, according to the Naidānas, it is so called because one thought it was equal to the *ṛc* through the root *as* (to throw or cast). [782]

7,12: *Gāyatrī* is derived from the root *gai*, meaning "to praise," or it signifies "threefold movement" (*tri-gamanā*), as the Brāhmaṇa states: "She sprang forth from the mouth of the one who was singing. 7,12: *Uṣṇik* is so called because she has "heated up" (*utsnātā*) or because she comes from the root *snih*, meaning "to shine" (*kānti-karmaṇaḥ*); or it is a figurative expression (*aupamika*) meaning "she who wears a turban" (*uṣṇīsinī*). 7,12: *Uṣṇīsa* is derived from the root *snā*.

7.12: *Kakubh* becomes *kakubhinī*. 7.12: *Kakubh* and *kubja* derive from either the root *kuja-* or the root *ubja-*. 7.12: Regarding *anuṣṭubh*, it is because of its "repeated praising" (*anu-stobhana*). The Brāhmaṇa states: "[One] repeatedly praises the *gāyatrī*, which consists of three feet, with a fourth foot. [782–783]
7.12: [It is called] *bṛhatī* because of its expansion (*paribarhaṇa*). 7.12: The *paṅkti* consists of five feet (*pañcapadā*).
7.12: The *triṣṭubh* chants (*stobhati*) with its final foot (*uttara-pada*).
7.12: "The *triṣṭubh* should be threefold; it is the most-pervading meter, the *triṣṭubh* is the thunderbolt (*vajra*), and its praise is [the *stobha*]," so it is said.

7.12: "Because it praised three times, that is the *triṣṭubh*; you are the *triṣṭubh*," thus it is known. 7.13: The *jagatī* is the most-moving meter, or it is the movement of aquatic creatures; and the *Brāhmaṇa* says, "Moving about, he created."
7,13: *Virāj* is so called because of shining forth (*virājanāt*), or because of overcoming (*virādhanāt*), or because of reaching far (*viprāpanāt*).
7,13: It is *virājanāt* when it has complete syllables; *virādhanāt* when it has deficient syllables; and *viprāpanāt* when it has excessive syllables. 7,13:
"Ant-like in the middle" (*pipīlikamadhyā*) is a metaphorical expression.
7,13: [This refers to] the action of movement belonging to the *pipīlikā-pelata* [meter]. 7,13: Thus these deities have been enumerated. 7,13:

Most of them are recipients of hymns (*sūkta-bhāj*), recipients of oblations (*havis-bhāj*), and recipients of verses (*rc-bhāj*); some are recipients of indeclinables (*nipāta-bhāj*). [The verses are sung to Sūrya beginning with "udv eti" (RV 7.60.1ff.), numbering four and a half. 7,13, ḍ. 787; Cf. Bḍ. 6,5.
7,13: [The particle *hi* is of two kinds:
7,13: it occurs either in common praise together with other deities, or as a term belonging to the *naighaṇṭuka* class.
7,13: Regarding its occurrence in common praise, for example: "The ordainer (*vidhātṛ*) and the creator (*dhātṛ*)," which has been explained.
7,13: This is its occurrence in a verse addressed to many deities:
"Of King Soma.
In this [verse], the Ordainer is praised together with Soma and others by way of commonality.
7,13: Furthermore, by way of the *naighaṇṭuka* (lexicographical) section, it is as follows: "The earth has been explained.
This is its occurrence as a derivative form (*nipāta*) in a verse addressed to Indra and Agni:
"O Indra and Agni, on the highest earth... and so forth.
7,13: The earth is not praised here as being common to both Indra and Agni together;

rather, it is mentioned merely as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of Indra and Agni themselves. (Durga 788; cf. Nirukta 11.11–12.12, 30–31). 7,13: [Now, this other method of interpreting *nipātas* is to be disregarded, namely: that which is strictly etymological (*atyanta-naighaṇṭuka*) regarding the designation of a deity, and that which is not strictly etymological (*anatyanta-naighaṇṭuka*). (Durga 788)

7,13: Furthermore, having joined them with their characteristic appellations, he enjoins the oblation: "To Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra; to Indra, the overcomer of Vṛtra; to Indra, the releaser from distress. [786] 7,13: Some also recite these [names], but because they are more numerous than the traditional recitation, that which has become a conventional designation—being a preeminent praise—is what they recite.
[786] 7,13: Furthermore, by means of [these] actions, the seer praises the deities: "The slayer of Vṛtra, the destroyer of forts," and so forth. [786]

7.13: Some authorities also recite these [names], but they are more numerous than the standard recitation; however, those are merely descriptive epithets of that name, just as one might say, "Give rice to the hungry Brāhmaṇa," "ointment to the one who has bathed," or "water to the thirsty.
7.14: Now, therefore, we shall proceed in due order.
Fire (Agni) and the Earth (Pṛthivī) are its abodes; we shall explain him first.

7.14: Why is he called Agni? Because he is a leader (*agranī*); he is led to the forefront in sacrifices; he leads the limbs [of the sacrifice] while bending them together. 7.14: "He is *aknopana*," says Sthaulāṣṭhīvi; he does not cause to drip (*knopayati*), that is, he does not cause to become oily.
7.14: Śākapūṇi says he is born from three verbal roots: from *ita*, from *akta*, and from *dagdha*—that is, from what has been led, from what has been smeared, and from what has been burnt.
7.14: He indeed takes the vowel *a* from the root *eti*; the consonant *g* from either *añjati* or *dahati*, followed by the prefix *niḥ*.
Of this [word], there is this [verse]: 7.15:
"I praise Agni, the domestic priest, the god, the officiating priest of the sacrifice... [RV 1.1.1]
7,15: "The Hotṛ, the best bestower of treasures"—7,15: "I praise Agni; I entreat Agni. 7,15: *īḍ* is a verb meaning to implore or to honor.
7.15: The domestic priest (*purohita*) and the sacrifice (*yajña*) have already been explained.

A god (*deva*) is so called because he gives (*dāna*), or because he causes to swell (*pīpana*), or because he shines (*dyotana*), or because his abode is in heaven (*dyu-sthāna*). That which is a god is a deity (*devatā*).
7,15: He is the Hotṛ, the invoker.
7,15: Aurnavābha says that he is the Hotṛ because he performs the oblation (*juhoti*). 7,15: *Ratnadhātama*: the best bestower of jewels, that is, the most excellent giver of delightful riches.
Regarding this, there is another verse:
"Agni is to be praised by the ancient seers and by the present ones as well;
may he bring the gods here."
7.16: "May that Agni—who was to be invoked (or praised) by the ancient seers and by us who are newer—bring the gods here.
7.16: One should not think, "This alone is Agni," for these two other lights are also called Agnis. 7.16: Following that is the middle one.
7,17: "They flow toward Agni like beautiful women smiling as they go to a common gathering;
the streams of clarified butter reach the fuel-sticks, and Jātavedas, delighting in them, eagerly accepts them.
7,17: They bow down toward him with one mind, like women [approaching a lover].
7,17: *samānam* means "from the same" (*samanāt*) or "from equality" (*sammānāt*).
7,17: "The beautiful women, smiling, [approach] Agni"—this is a simile (*aupamika*).
7,17: "Streams of ghee" means "streams of water."

7,17: *samidhaḥ* means "they are kindling" (*nasanti*) or "they obtain" (*āpnoti*). *Namati* means "he bends" or "he performs an action. 7,17: *jātavedāḥ*, being pleased with them, desires them. 7,17: *haryati* has the sense of seeking to obtain; as in the expression *viharyati*.

7,17: "The honeyed wave has risen from the ocean"—this [verse] they consider to refer to Āditya; and there is also the Brāhmaṇa passage: "For he rises from the waters of the ocean. Furthermore, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage stating: "Agni is all the deities."
7,17: The following [verses] are for the further etymological explanation of that. 7,18: "They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni; and he is the divine, fair-winged Garuḍa.
The sages speak of the One Being as manifold; they call him Agni, Yama, and Mātariśvan" (Ṛgveda 1.164.46).
7.18: The wise speak of this very Agni as the Great Self, the one Self manifoldly;
[they call him] Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni, and the celestial Garuḍa—the celestial one who moves through the sky.
7,18: [He is] Garuḍa because he devours (*garaṇavat*), or because his self is heavy (*guru-ātman*), or because he is the Great Self (*mahā-ātman*).
7,18: He who partakes of the hymn (*sūkta*) and for whom the oblation (*havis*) is prepared—he is indeed this Agni.

8,12: "The three goddesses. There are three goddesses; regarding them, this [verse] occurs: 8,13: "May Bhāratī come quickly to our sacrifice, and Iḷā, being mindful here like Manu; may the three goddesses—Sarasvatī and those of skillful works—sit upon this pleasant sacrificial grass (barhis)."

8,13: and may Ilā, perceiving here like a human being, [be present].
8,13: "May the three goddesses—Sarasvatī and the two of good deeds—sit upon this pleasant sacrificial grass.

Regarding *Tvaṣṭṛ*, the etymologists say he is so called because "he quickly attains" (*tūrṇam aśnute*). Alternatively, it may derive from *tviṣ*, meaning "to shine," or from *tvakṣ*, meaning "to fashion. Of him, there is this verse: 8,14:
"He who, as the progenitor of these two, Heaven and Earth, has adorned all beings with forms."
8,14: O Hotṛ, impelled today, you who are more skilled in sacrifice, worship here as a knower the god Tvaṣṭṛ.

8,14: He who created these two, Heaven and Earth, the progenitors, and all beings with their forms—O Hotṛ, impelled today, you who are more skilled in sacrifice, worship here as a knower that god Tvaṣṭṛ.
They say that Tvaṣṭṛ belongs to the intermediate realm, and he is traditionally recited in the middle station.
8,14: Śākapūṇi says it is Agni. 8,14: Of him there is this other [verse]: 8,15:
"The lovely one, belonging to the waters, grows up within them; upright in the lap of those that are bent, he increases, self-glorious."
8,15: Both [worlds] were afraid of Tvaṣṭṛ as he was being born; turning toward him, they both delight the lion.
8,15: He has become manifest from his appearance.
8,15: He, the beautiful one, grows among them.
8,15: He who moves beautifully becomes straight when he abandons crookedness; he is exalted when he rises upward. 8,15: He is self-glorious, glorious by his own nature, in the place of worship.
8,15: Both worlds trembled with fear at the birth of the Fashioner.
8,15: The two facing ones sing in response to the lion;
they are either heaven and earth, or day and night, or the two banks.
8,15: The two facing ones serve the conquering lion in response.
8,15: Vanaspati has been explained.
8,15: This is its [verse].
8,16: Vanaspati has been explained.
8,16: Regarding this, there is this [verse]:
8,17: "Release [the victim] by yourself, anointing it, at the proper time, into the path of the gods for the oblations.
May Vanaspati, the divine Agni the immolator, and Agni—make the offering savory with honey and ghee."
8,17: Release [the victim] by yourself, anointing yourself, as the food of the gods, at every season, at the proper time after time.
8,17: May these three—the tree (vanaspati), the immolator (śamitṛ), and the divine Agni—make the oblation palatable with honey and with clarified butter.
8,17: What is that tree? Kāṭhaka says it is the sacrificial post (yūpa); Śākapūṇi says it is Agni. Regarding this, there is another verse:
8,18: "The seekers of the gods anoint you, O Lord of the Forest, with divine honey at the sacrifice;
whether you stand upright bestowing wealth here, or whether you dwell in the lap of this Mother Earth.
The seekers of the gods, desiring the deities, anoint you, O Lord of the Forest, at the sacrifice with divine honey and with clarified butter."
When you shall stand upright,
you will grant us riches;
or when your dwelling has been prepared in the lap of this mother.
8,18: "Agni," says Śākapūṇi; regarding him, there is this other [verse]:
8,19: "O Vanaspati, golden-leaved, you carry the oblations to the gods from of old for their sake.
Having harnessed them with the cord in a clockwise direction, you convey them by the straightest paths of Truth."
8,19: To the gods belongs the oblation of the Vanaspati, whose leaves are golden, whose leaves are truth; or rather, it may be for the sake of comparison, meaning "whose leaves are gold-colored.
8,19: From of old has been your purpose; that ancient purpose of yours is the one we proclaim to you. 8,19:
Carry [the sacrifice] along the paths of the sacrifice—straightest, most truthful, and most luminous through the mid-air.
8.19: Or rather, [it is] "by those most full. 8.19: Of this, there is another verse.

8.20: "O Lord of the Forest, having bound [the horse] with a girth made of flour, you who know the ways, carry the offerings to the gods according to their portions; and proclaim the giver among the immortals."
Having bound [the horse] with a girth of the lord of the forest, most beautiful in form,
you who know the ways and understand all things, carry the gods to the sacrifice, O giver of the oblation.
And announce the donor among the immortal gods.
8.20: *svāhākṛtayaḥ* / 8.20:
*svāhā* means either *su-āha* ("he has spoken well") or *svā-svac-āha* ("he has spoken what is his own").
Or [it means] "he has spoken his own [truth]," or "he offers the oblation well-sacrificed. Regarding these, there is this verse:
8,21: "As soon as he was born, Agni measured out the sacrifice; he became the leader of the gods.
At the direction of this Hotṛ, in the speech of Ṛta, let the gods eat the oblation consecrated with Svāhā!
8,21: As soon as he was born, Agni fashioned the sacrifice; he became the one who goes before the gods.
8.21: "May the gods eat the oblation offered with the cry of *svāhā* in the mouth, in the speech, and in the direction of this Hotṛ of the *ṛta*.
Thus these *āprī* deities have been enumerated.
Now, what are the deities of the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s?"

8,21: Some say they belong to Agni. 8,22: "O gods, grant me the prayājas and the anuyājas exclusively as my portion of the oblation, full of vigor; [grant me] the clarified butter of the waters and the essence of the plants; and may there be long life for Agni."
"May the *prayājas* and *anuyājas* be for you alone; may the portions of the oblation be full of vigor.
O Agni, let the sacrifice and Yama be yours entirely; let the four quarters bow down to you.
Indeed, the *prayājas* belong to Agni, and the *anuyājas* belong to Agni.
8,22: And thus says the Brāhmaṇa. 8,22: "The meters are the deities," so it is said elsewhere. 8,22: "The Prayājas are indeed the meters; the Anuyājas are the meters," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
8,22: "The seasons are the deities"—this is another [view].
8,22: And there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "The fore-offerings (prayāja) are indeed the seasons; the after-offerings (anuyāja) are the animal sacrifice.
8,22: "The vital breaths are the deities"—this is yet another [view].
8,22: "The *prayāja*s are indeed the out-breaths (*prāṇa*); the *anuyāja*s are the in-breaths (*apāna*)," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
8,22: But the established position is that they belong to Agni (*āgneya*).
8,22: The other [explanation] is merely figurative (*bhakti-mātra*).

8,22: For what purpose, then, is this stated? It is known from tradition: "Whichever deity for whom the oblation has been taken up, one should meditate upon that deity mentally when about to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call. These are the eleven *āprī* hymns.

8,22: Among these, those belonging to Vasiṣṭha, Mātra, Vadhryaśva, and Gṛtsamada are accompanied by the Nārāśaṃsa verses. Those belonging to Medhātithi, Dīrghatamas, and the Praiṣika are accompanied by both [the Nārāśaṃsa and the Tanūnapāt].
All others are accompanied by the Tanūnapāt verses; they are accompanied by the Tanūnapāt verses.
9,1: Now, we shall enumerate those beings who have the earth as their abode and receive praise.
Among them, the horse comes first.
The horse has already been explained; regarding it, there is this [verse]:
9,2: "The horse is the drawer of the easy chariot; the frogs are the inviters to laughter.
The male frog desires the hairy female frog. Flow, O Indu, for Indra. 9,2:
The horse is the drawer (vodhā).
9,2: "One who draws easily. 9,2: "One who draws a chariot. 9,2: "Sukha" is a name for what is auspicious.
9,2: It is auspicious and meritorious; it becomes well-satisfied, or it goes to a state of being well-satisfied.
9,2: Or it means "these [vows] have been abandoned";
9,2: or "he is a protector" or "a guardian"; 9,2: or "he incurs a deficiency."
9,2: *vāri-vārayati*.
9,2: *māna* has been explained; of it, this [verse] occurs:
9,3: "May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, Āyu, Indra, Ṛbhukṣan, and the Maruts not look with disdain upon us."
9,3: "When we shall proclaim the heroic deeds of the prize-winning steed, born of the gods, in the assembly.

9,3: "When we shall proclaim the heroic deeds of the prize-winning steed, born of the gods, the swift runner, in the sacrifice and the assembly—may you, O Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, Āyu, Vāyu, Indra, the dweller in the wide realm, and the King of the Ṛbhus—or the Maruts—not hold us in contempt.
9,3: "The bird is able to lead itself upward."
Or, "May he be able to roar";
or, "May he be able to strike down";
or, "May he be a bringer of welfare from every side."
9,3: Or [it is derived] from the root *śak* (to be able).
9,3: Of this, there is this [verse]: 9,4: "Crying out, proclaiming his birth, he sends forth his voice like a rower propelling a boat."
9,4: And may you be an auspicious bird; let no all-pervading distress find you. 9,4:
He has cried out, proclaiming his birth; as is his sound, so he utters his name, like one who impels speech, impelling a boat. 9,4:
And may you be an auspicious bird, O bringer of beautiful blessings.

9,4: *Maṅgalam* is so called because it proclaims what is beneficial (*nirati*) for one's purpose, or because it swallows away (*girati*) what is harmful (*anartha*). 9,4: *Aṅgalam* is like a limb (*aṅga*).
9,4: The etymologists (*nairukta*) say it is that which immerses (*majjayati*) the ripening of karma.
9,4: Or [let it be said]: "May it not come to me.
And may no affliction from any quarter find you.
Kapiñjala called out to Gṛtsamada as he had risen for his purpose.

9,4: There is this verse expressing that [meaning]: 9,5: "Speak auspiciously from the south; speak auspiciously from the north; speak auspiciously to us from the east; speak auspiciously from the west, O Kapiñjala! This [verse] is explained by its own liturgical formula (nigada).
9,5: Gṛtsamada is one who possesses keen intelligence (*gṛtsa-madana*). 9,5: *Gṛtsa* is a name for one who is wise.
9,5: It is derived from the verbal root *gṛ*, which has the sense of praising.

9,5: [The word *maṇḍūka*] is derived from *majjūkā*, meaning "to dive"; or from *madati*, a verb whose action is "to rejoice"; or from *mandati*, a verb whose action is "to satisfy. According to the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇāḥ*), it is derived from *mandayati*.
9,5: "Manda" means their dwelling place;
or, "manda" is derived from the root *mad* (to exhilarate) or *mud* (to rejoice).
Regarding them, this [verse] occurs:
"Having lain for a year, the Brāhmaṇas who observe their vows,
the frogs, have uttered forth speech inspired by Parjanya.
Having lain for a year, the Brāhmaṇas who observe their vows remained silent.
Alternatively, it may be used in the sense of a comparison, as in "like Brāhmaṇas observing their vows. The frogs uttered speech that was pleasing to Parjanya;
Vasiṣṭha, desiring rain, praised Parjanya.
9,6: The frogs rejoiced in him.
9,6: Having seen the frogs rejoicing, he praised them.
9,6: There is this ṛc which expresses that very thing.
9,7: "Speak forth, O Mandūki; speak for rain, O Tāduri!
Swim in the middle of the lake, having spread out your four feet. This [verse] is explained by its own recitation (nigada).
9,7: The dice.
"Either 'they have attained these,' or 'they have attained by means of these'—
of them, this [verse] occurs."
9,8: "The dangling, great fruits, born in the wind and rolling upon the slope, exhilarate me.
Like a draught of Soma from Mount Mūjavat, the wakeful Vibhīdaka fruit has pleased me. 9,8: The dangling, great fruits of the Vibhīdaka tree exhilarate me.
9,8: Born in the wind, produced in the wind;
moving in the desert. The desert is "nirṛṇa," for it is a place where there is no repayment (*apārṇa*) from the root *ṛṇāti* (to owe).
9,8: Or rather, [it is called] *apārā* because the plants have departed from this [place].
9,8: It is like the consumption of Soma from Mount Mūjavat. 9,8: *Maujavata* means born on Mount Mūjavat.
9,8: The mountain is Mūjavat; [it is] Muñjavat. 9,8: Muñja is that from which the *isīkā* is released.
9,8: *Isīkā* is derived from the root *iṣ*, meaning "to go."
9,8: This other *isīkā* also [arises] from this very same [source].
9,8: The *vibhīdaka* [is so called] because of its splitting (*vibhedana*). 9,8: The *jāgṛvi* [is so called] because of its wakefulness (*jāgarana*).
9,8: He covered for me;
9,8: he praises them with the first [verse], and censures them with the subsequent ones;
9,8: they declare this to be the seer’s composition concerning Ṛsi, who was defeated at dice.
9,8: The pressing-stones (*grāvāṇaḥ*) are so called from the root *han* (to strike), or from *gṛ* (to praise), or from *grah* (to seize).
9,8: Of these, there is this [verse]: 9,9: "Let these speak forth; let us speak forth; let speech be spoken for the speaking pressing-stones."
9,9: O mountains, O rocks, you who are swift together, bring forth a hymn, a shout for Indra, O Soma-pressers!
Let these speak out;
let us speak out!
9,9: Speak your voice to the pressing-stones as they speak;
when the stones, the mountains, have been pressed, O swift-acting ones, together with the Soma.
*Śloka* comes from the root *śru*, "to hear," and *ghoṣa* from the root *ghuṣ*, "to sound."
"Or [the mantra] beginning with *somino yūyam stha*; or [the mantra] beginning with *somino gṛheṣu*.
That mantra by which men are praised is the *nārāśaṃsa*."
9,9: Of him, this [verse] occurs:
9,10: "With inspired thought, I offer forth unceasing hymns of praise for Bhāvya, who dwells upon the river—the king who, desiring glory, swiftly measured out for me a thousand libations.
9,10: "With inspired thought, I offer forth unceasing hymns of praise for Bhāvya, who dwells upon the river—the king who, desiring glory, swiftly measured out for me a thousand libations."
9,10: "Not dull hymns" means not foolish or not meager.
A fool, being subject to [the power of] strength, becomes one who must be supported.
9,10: Or [it means] "the mother is sufficient for him";
or 9,10: "strength is for him";
or 9,10: "strength" is separated by a negation.
I offer with my mind, with the impulse of thought, with praise, or with wisdom. O King Bhāvayavya, who dwells upon the Sindhu river, you who have fashioned for me a thousand libations—
you are the unconquered king.
9,10: Or "not hurriedly";
9,10: Or "not hastening";
9,10: "Desiring praise."
9,11: Through connection with sacrifice, the king receives praise;
through connection with the king, the implements of war [are obtained].
Among these, the chariot is the first to arrive.
9,11: *Ratha* is derived from the root *raṃhati*, which has the sense of "motion.
Alternatively, it may come from *sthira-* with metathesis;
or [it means] "he stands rejoicing (*ramamāṇa*) upon this."
[The word *vanaspati*] is derived either from the root *rap* or from the root *ras*.
Regarding this, there is the following verse:
"O Lord of the Forest, may you have strong limbs; be our friend, furthering us and rich in heroes."
9,12: "You are bound with cow-hides; be firm! May your rider be victorious over those things to be conquered.
9,12: "O Lord of the Forest, be firm-limbed! Be our friend, a furtherer, a hero of good lineage, a hero of auspicious lineage!
9,12: "You are bound with cow-hides; be firm"—that is, take your stand.
9,12: May he who mounts you conquer all that is to be conquered.
9,12: "Dundubhi" is an imitation of sound; or it means "the tree has burst. 9,12: Or [it means] "the tree has been split."
9,12: Or [the root] *dundubhyati* may belong to the verbal root *śabd*, meaning "to sound. 9,12: Of this [root], there is this [verse]:
9,13: "Make the earth and the sky resound; let the world, established in many places, take heed of you."

O you who possess the drum, in harmony with Indra and the gods, drive the enemies far, even to the furthest distance. (RV 6.47.29) Cause the earth and the heavens to resound! Let the loud noise of you, who are manifold, be heard throughout all that is established—the stationary and the moving.
9,13: O you who resound with the drum, drive the enemies far away, even further away, along with Indra and the gods.
9,13: The quiver;
the repository of arrows.
Regarding this, there is this verse:

"He is the father of many; his sons are many. He makes a whizzing sound as he rushes into the fray. With quiver strapped to his back, he conquers all hosts and armies when he goes forth to battle" (Ṛgveda 6.75.5).
9,14: "He is the father of many; he has many sons"—this refers to the arrows. 9,14: "As if smiling while being uncovered. 9,14: Or it is an imitation of sound.

9,14: *saṅkāḥ* is derived from the root *sac*, preceded by the prefix *sam*, or from the root *kṛ*, also preceded by *sam*. 9,14: It has been explained that "bound upon the back, he conquers" means "impelled. 9,14: *Hastaghna* means "that which is struck in the hand."
Regarding this, there is this [verse]:
"Like a serpent with its coils, it encircles the arm, warding off the blow of the bowstring;
the hand-guard, knowing all the ways, as a man, shall protect the man from every side."
Like a snake, it encircles the arm with its coils, protecting [the hand] from being struck by the bowstring; the *hastaghna* (hand-killer) knows all forms of knowledge.
The term *pumān* (man) is derived from *purumanas* (having many thoughts), or from the root *puṃsati*.
The term *abhīśu* (rein) has already been explained.
Regarding them, there is this [verse]:
"Standing on the chariot, the skillful charioteer leads the horses forward wherever he desires. Admire the greatness of the reins; from behind, the traces follow according to the mind."
Standing on the chariot, the skillful charioteer—the excellent driver—leads the horses forward to wherever he desires.
I celebrate the greatness of the reins;
though they are behind, the traces follow the mind.
9,16: *dhanus* and *dhanvati* [are derived from a root] meaning "to go" or "to strike. From it, arrows (*iṣavaḥ*) fly forth. Regarding this, there is the following verse:
9,17: "With the bow may we win cattle, with the bow may we win the battle; with the bow may we win fierce conflicts.

The bow frustrates the desire of the enemy; with the bow may we conquer all directions. This [verse] is explained by its own recitation (*nigada*). 9,17: *Samadaḥ* means either "conflicts" from the root *ad* ("to eat"), or "rejoicings" from the root *mad* ("to rejoice").
9.17: [The word *jyā*] is derived either from the root *ji* (to conquer), or from *jināti* (to overcome), or because it "propels arrows.
9.17: Regarding this, there is this verse: 9.18: "As if they were speaking, they come close to the ear, embracing their dear friend."
Like a woman, this bowstring twangs upon the stretched bow, carrying [the warrior] across to victory in the encounter.
As if speaking, it comes to the ear; like an embrace for a dear friend, it clings to the arrow.
Like a woman, it twangs—that is, it makes a sound—upon the stretched bow; this bowstring carries [the warrior] across, leading him to the further shore in the encounter, that is, in battle.
9,18: [The word] *iṣu* belongs to the root *iṣ*, meaning "to go," or it means "killing.
Regarding this, there is the following verse:
9,19: "She wears a beautiful-feathered garment; her tooth is like a deer's; bound with cow-hides, she flies forth when discharged."
9,19: "Where men run together and apart, there may they grant us protection from arrows.
9,19: [The word] *vājān* [is used] with reference to the swift-feathered arrows. 9,19: Its teeth are made of deer-horn, or it comes from the root *mṛg* (to seek).
9,19: "Bound with cow-hides, it flies forth when discharged"—this has been explained.
9,19: Where men rush together and flee apart, there may the arrows grant us protection and refuge in battles.
9,19: They call the horse-whip a *kaśā*.
9,19: A whip reveals fear to the horse;
or [it is so called] because it follows after the act of plowing (*kṛs*);
speech, moreover, reveals meanings.
9,19: [The verse] beginning with *khaśayā*; 9,19: [the verse] beginning with *krośateḥ vā*;
9,19: this [verse] belongs to *aśvakaśā*.
9,20: "They strike their flanks; they beat upon their haunches. O wise horse-whip, urge the horses on in the battles! 9,20:
They strike their ridges, their thighs, and their haunches.
9,20: *Sakthi* is derived from *sacati*; the body is attached to it. 9,20: And it strikes against the hips (*jaghanāni*). 9,20: *Jaghana* is derived from *jaṅghanyate* (to strike repeatedly).
9,20: O you who are wise with the horse-whip, whose minds are fully developed, urge on the horses in battles, in encounters, and in combats!
9,20: "The mortar—whether it be the wide-maker, or the upward-hollowed, or the strength-maker—said, 'Make wide space for me! and thus it became the mortar."
9,20: "And this wide-working one they call 'the mortar' by a cryptic name," so says the Brāhmaṇa. 9,20:
Of it there is this verse:
9,21: "For whenever you, O little mortar, are yoked in every house..."
9,21: "Here, speak most brilliantly, like the drum of those who sacrifice"—this [verse] is explained by its *nigada* (liturgical formula).
9,22: "The bull rains down offspring," or rather, he rains down semen (*retas*) excessively;
because his action is that of a bull (*vṛṣan*), he is called a bull (*vṛṣabha*).
Regarding him, there is this [verse]:
"Approaching him, they made the bull bellow loudly in the midst of the contest;
by him, Mudgala won a thousand well-nourished cattle, along with a hundred, in the prize-winning race."
9,23: "They approached him, crying out"—this has been explained.
9,23: "They made the bull urinate in the midst of the contest," or [it means] "of one who is winning in the contest" (*ājivanasya*), or "of one who is moving in the contest" (*ājavanasya*).
9,23: By that [means], they [made] that well-providing king.
*Subharva* means "one who eats.
Mudgala won a thousand *subharvas* of cattle in a contest (*pradhana*). *Pradhana* is a name for battle, so called because wealth is scattered therein.
9,23: A *drughana* is a mallet made of wood.
Regarding this, they relate an ancient legend (*itihāsa*):
the seer Mudgala Bhārmyaśva, having yoked both a bull and a wooden mallet, engaged in battle and won the contest.
Regarding this, there is a Ṛc that expresses it:
"Behold this one, the yoke-mate of the bull, the wooden beam lying in the middle of the pole—by means of which Mudgala won a hundred thousand cattle in the contests for booty. (RV 10.102.8)
9,24: Behold this one, the companion of the bull, the wooden beam lying in the middle of the pole.
With it, Mudgala won hundreds and thousands of cattle in the contests for booty. "Pṛtanājya" is a name for battle.
9,24: *Pṛtanāṇaja* is so called because he was born from armies (*pṛtanā*) or because he conquers them (*jayana*).

9,24: *Mudgala* means "possessing beans" (*mudgavān*), or "swallower of beans" (*mudgagila*), or "he swallows intoxication" (*madanaṃ gilati*), or "swallower of intoxication" (*madagila*), or "swallower of joy" (*mudagila*).
9,24: *Bhārmyaśva* is the son of *Bhṛmyaśva*.
9,24: *Bhṛmyaśva* means one whose horses are swift (*bhṛmi*), or [one who] bears the horse (*aśva-bharana*).
9,24: *Pituḥ* is a name for food.
9,24: It is derived from the root *pā* (to protect), or *pā* (to drink), or *pyai* (to swell).
Regarding him, there is this verse:
"Sing now the praise-song to the food, the great ordinance,
the powerful strength, by whose vigor Trita shattered Vṛtra limb from limb."
9,25: I praise that food, the sustainer of great strength. *Tavisī* is a name for strength;
or it is derived from the root *tavati*, which means "to increase."
9,25: By whose power and strength Trita—Trita, who dwells in the three places, Indra—shatters Vṛtra, whose joints are severed. 9,25: The rivers have been explained.
Regarding these [rivers], there is this [verse]:
"May Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Śutudrī, Paruṣṇī, Asiknī, Marudvṛdhā, Vitastā, Ārjīkīyā, and Susomā accept this hymn of praise of mine. (RV 10.75.5)
9,26: O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Śutudrī, and Paruṣṇī, accept this hymn of praise from me!
9,26: And you, Asiknī together with Marudvṛdhā, Vitastā, Ārjīkīyā, and Susomā—listen! This is the meaning of the verse as a whole.
Now follows the etymological explanation of each word.
9,26: From going to the Gaṅgā; or [she is called] Yamunā because she goes with the young women, or because she goes apart/separately; [and] Sarasvatī.
9,26: *Saras* is a name for water. 9,26: It possesses flowing (*sarteḥ tadvatī*), [the Ṛgvedic verse] regarding water.
9,26: *Śutudrī* means "she who causes the *śudra*s to flee," or "she who flows swiftly like one who has been quickly pierced."
9,26: They call her Irāvatī, Paruṣṇī; she is Parvavatī, Bhasvatī, and Kutilagāminī.
9,26: She is Asiknī, Aśuklā, and Asitā. "Sita" is a name for color; its negation is "asita."
9,26: All rivers are strengthened by the Maruts; the Maruts cause them to swell.
9,26: The Vitastā is unburnt; 9,26: the great families have increased. (9,26)
9,26: Regarding the Vipāś, they say it is "ārjīkīyā," because it originates from the Ṛjīka mountain, or because it flows straight.
9,26: It is called Vipāś either because of its tossing about (vipātana) or because of its binding away (vipāśana).
9,26: Or because of the release from bonds. 9,26: The fetters were loosened here for Vasiṣṭha as he was about to die;
therefore it is called Vipāś, for previously it was Uruñjirā.
9,26: When the rivers, the streams of good Soma, impel her forward, she becomes the Sindhu;
"Sindhu" [is so called] because of her flowing.
9,27: "O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss; grant us strength."
9,27: For the great battle, for seeing; 9,27: "O Waters, you indeed are the source of happiness; grant us food, and for our great battle and for delightful sight."
9,27: They suck [the essence] from the herbs (*oṣadhīḥ*), or they suck [it] while it is present (*osati*). Or, they suck away the fault (*doṣam*).
Of these, this [verse] occurs:
9,28: "The plants that were born first, three ages before the gods—now I celebrate the hundred and seven abodes of those tawny ones. 9,28:
Those plants that were born first, three ages before the gods...
9,28: Now I think of those of the Babhru clan— those of the brown color, or perhaps those who carry, or those who bring—
the hundred and seven abodes.
9,28: There are three kinds of abodes (*dhāma*): places, names, and births. 9,28: Here, "births" is what is intended. 9,28:
Or rather, there are seven hundred vital points (*marman*) of a person; they place her within them.
9,28: Night has been explained.
9,28: Of it, this [verse] occurs:
9,28: *Āpaḥ* [is derived] from the root *āp* (to obtain).
Regarding them, there is this [verse]:
"O Night, you have filled the earthly realm with your abodes, O daughter of the Pitṛs. Expansive, you spread out to the seat of heaven; darkness rolls back against you. (RV 10.127.1)
9,29: O Night, you fill the earthly realm and the stations of the intermediate space; you are the seat of heaven, vast and great.
9,29: You stand apart; the fierce darkness of the mid-air revolves.
9,29: O Forest One, wife of the forest!
The forest is without end compared to the village.
9,29: "It becomes a place of rest," so it is said;
regarding this, there is this [verse]:
9,30: "O forest-dweller, O forest-dweller, you who are as if vanishing away!"
"9,30: Why do you not ask for the village? Does fear not find you? 9,30: He addresses her as "O Forests!
9,30: "O Forests, you who are like the woods, you vanish as if into the distance."
9,30: Why do you not ask the way to the village? 9,30: Is it as if fear does not find you? 9,30: Or, *iva* may signify "fear" itself.
9.30: Faith. Because of faith. Regarding this, there is this [verse]: 9.31: "By faith the fire is kindled; by faith the oblation is offered."
9,31: We proclaim faith upon the head of fortune with our speech.
9,31: By means of faith, Agni is properly kindled; 9,31: by means of faith, the oblation is properly offered.
9,31: We announce faith upon the head of Bhaga, the portion-giver, that is, upon his primary limb, by means of our speech.
9,31: The Earth has been explained.
9,31: This is her [verse]:
"O Earth, be pleasant for us, thornless, and a place of rest;
grant us wide-spreading shelter.
O Bhaga, may the Earth be comfortable for us, thornless, and a place of rest.
9,32: *Ṛkṣaraḥ* is [the horse] Kaṇṭhaka; it comes from the root *ṛcchati*. 9,32: *Kaṇṭakaḥ* may be [derived] from *kaṇṭapaḥ*, or from *kṛntati*, or from *kaṇṭati*, which has the sense of "going.
9,32: He becomes most exalted (*udgatatamaḥ*).
9,32: Grant us protection;
may they grant us a refuge broad on all sides.
Apvā has been explained.
Regarding her, there is this verse (9,32):
"O Apvā, bewitching the minds of these men, seize their limbs and depart!
Advance against them; burn them with sorrows in their hearts! Let the enemies be possessed by blinding darkness. (9,33)
9,33: Bewildering the minds and understandings of these people, seize their limbs, O Apvā!
9,33: Go forth!
9,33: Advance!
9,33: Burn their hearts with sorrows; let the enemies be enveloped by blinding darkness.
9,33: Agnāyī is the wife of Agni. This [verse] belongs to her.
9,34: "I invoke Indrāṇī here, and Varuṇānī for well-being; I invoke Agnāyī for the drinking of Soma. This [verse] is explained by its own recitation (nigada).
9,35: Now, therefore, follow eight pairs.
9,35: The mortar and pestle. 9,35: The mortar has been explained.
9,35: The pestle moves repeatedly.
Regarding these two, there is this verse:
"O most excellent winners of booty, you who are ever-yielding; for they are held aloft, devouring the soma-juices like two tawny steeds."

9,36: Of the foods that must be exerted for, you two are the greatest sharers; for your two bay steeds (*harī*) are carried aloft as if they were eating the foods. 9,36: [The two] Havirdhānas are the repositories of the oblations (*havis*).
Regarding these two, there is this verse:
9,37: "May the gods worthy of sacrifice, free from malice, sit upon your lap for the drinking of Soma here today.

9,37: May the gods worthy of sacrifice—those who accomplish the sacrifice—sit upon your lap, that is, upon the place of sitting, or [upon you] who are not to be harmed, for the drinking of Soma here today.
9.37: Dyāvāpṛthivī (Heaven and Earth) has been explained.
9.37: Of these two, this [verse] occurs:
9.38: "May Heaven and Earth today [grant us] this successful [prayer], which touches the sky..."
9,38: "May they present the sacrifice among the gods.
9,38: May Heaven and Earth present this our sacrifice today—this means of accomplishment that reaches unto heaven—among the gods.
9,38: The Vipāś and Śutudrī have been explained.
Regarding these two, there is this verse:
"From the lap of the mountains, eager as they are, hastening like two unbridled horses,
licking each other like two bright mother-cows, the Vipāś and Śutudrī flow with their waters."
From the lap of the mountains, from their embrace; longing, desiring;
like horses that have been unyoked—or so it is said.
9,39: Or, it is [derived] from the root *vi-ṣad* (to sink down).
9,39: From *hāsamāna*.
9,39: The root *hās* is used in the sense of rivalry (*spardhā*).
Rejoicing like two beautiful, shining cows licking each other, the Vipāś and Śutudrī rush forward with their waters. Or they are like two bow-strings,
two bow-ends.
9,39: Or two forest-dwellers;
9,39: or two enemies.
Regarding these two, there is this [verse]:
"Moving together like a woman to her lover, may they bear [the arrow] in their lap like a mother her son;
may these two bow-ends, acting in concert and quivering, pierce the enemies and the foes.
Moving together as if with one mind like a woman, may they bear [the arrow] in their lap, in the space between them, like a mother her son.
May these two bow-ends, acting in concert, strike down the enemies; may they drive away the foes. Śuna and Sīra: Śuna is Vāyu.
9,40: *Śu* [is so called] because it moves in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). 9,40: *Sīra* is the Āditya, from the root *sar* (to move).
Regarding these two, there is this [verse]:
"O Śunāsīrau, may you two enjoy this speech; with that milk which you created in heaven, sprinkle upon this [earth]. This is the explanation of the *nigada*.
The two goddesses are the "delighters," the two divine ones who cause delight.
"9,41: *Dyāvāpṛthivī* (Heaven and Earth), or rather, day and night;
9,41: *Sasyam ca samā ca* (the crop and the year), so says Kāthakya. 9,41: For these two, this is the formal summons (*sampraisha*)."

9,42: "The two divine, joyous ones, the repositories of wealth; of these two, one drives away sins and hostilities, while the other brings desirable riches to the sacrificer. May they both partake of the gift of wealth for the sake of the seeker of wealth. Sacrifice! 9,42: "The two divine, joyous ones" means the two goddesses who are sources of delight. "The repositories of wealth" means the two who bestow riches. Of these two, one drives away misfortunes and hostilities.
9,42: Another brings desirable riches for the sacrificer, for the winning of wealth and for the bestowing of wealth.
9,42: "Sacrifice! is the summons. 9,42: O divine ones, you two are the offerings of strength.
9,42: "The two goddesses, Ūrjā and Āhvānī.
Or, "Heaven and Earth," or "Day and Night," according to Kāthakya;
or "The Crop and the Year," according to Kātyaka.

9,42: This is the *saṃpraiṣa* (direction) for those two: 9,43: "O divine *ūrjāhutī* (oblations of strength)! May one bring food and strength; may the other bring the shared meal and the shared drink. May we, cherishing the old with the new, and the new with the old, be [prosperous]. O *ūrjāhutī*, you who are strengthening that strength, bestow it; enjoy the gift of wealth for the sake of obtaining wealth!—*Perform the sacrifice!*"

The two goddesses are the offerings of strength (*ūrja-āhuti*); the two goddesses are the summoners of strength. One brings food and essence; the other brings them both repeatedly. Another [brings] eating together and drinking together.
May we, cherishing the old with the new,
and the new with the old,
partake of that nourishment; may the two [Heaven and Earth], being strengthened by the oblation of strength, bestow it for the winning of wealth.
9,43: And for the sake of bestowing wealth;
9,43: "Let them partake," "let them drink," or "let them desire";
9,43: "Sacrifice!"—this is the *saṃpraiṣa* (the call for sacrifice); "Sacrifice!"—this is the *saṃpraiṣa*.
10.1: Now, therefore, [we shall discuss] the deities belonging to the middle station.
Of these, Vāyu is the first to arrive.
Vāyu [is so called] either from the root *vā* or from *veti*, both of which belong to the class of roots meaning "to go."
10.1: Regarding the word *eter*, Sthaulāṣṭhīvi says that the letter *v* is meaningless.
10.1: Of this, there is the following [verse]:
10.2: "Come quickly, O beautiful one; here are the Soma juices, well-prepared."
"Drink of them; hear our invocation.
(RV 10.2) "O Vāyu, come hither, O beautiful one! These Soma juices have been prepared for you; drink of them and hear our call.
Who else but Madhyama could have spoken thus?
10,2: Of this, there is another [verse]:
10,3: "The well-wheeled chariot-horses, rushing toward the powerful Indra, shall bear him on, seeking renown;
never indeed shall the nectar of Vāyu be exhausted."

10.3: May the chariot-horses, having been harnessed to the chariot with beautiful wheels, carry forward Indra—who is rushing forth and exerting his strength—as the driver of the chariot; may they, moving straight on, bring straight toward him both new and old food.
"Śrava" is a name for food, because it is heard (śrūyate). And let there be for him a portion of this [food] so that he does not fail.
10.3: Some say that Indra is the primary deity, while others say it is a Vedic lexicon (naighaṇṭuka) concerning the action of Vāyu; another view holds that both are primary deities;
and [the name] Varuṇa is derived from the root *vṛ*, meaning "he covers."
Regarding this, there is a verse concerning him:
"Varuṇa" [is so called] because he obstructs the waters in the intermediate space; indeed, he is Vāyu himself.
10,4: "Varuṇa has released the water-skin with its opening downward toward heaven, earth, and the intermediate space;
with it, the king of the entire world moistens the ground as rain moistens barley. 10,4:
Varuṇa [released] the water-skin, the cloud, with its opening turned downward.
10,4: Water is *kavana*; that [water] is contained within it.
10,4: Water is also called *kavandha*.
10,4: The root *bandh* is used in the sense of being hidden or concealed.
10,4: And he emits his unconfined [semen] upon heaven and earth and the great intermediate space.
By that, the king of the entire world moistens the earth as rain moistens barley.
This is his *ārā* verse.

10.5: "Him with a song of common intent, and with the hymns of the fathers, with the praises of Nābhāka—at the rising of the rivers, he who has seven sisters, he is the central one. May all others perish!
I praise him with my own song, with a unified voice—through singing, through praise, with the meditative hymns of the fathers, and with the laudations of Nābhāka.
10.5: There was a seer named Nābhāka, who, at the rising of these flowing waters, [was addressed] by the seven sisters with their words.
He is designated as "the Middle One," and he indeed becomes this very one. May all others perish! 10.5: May all others perish! 10.5: May all others perish!
10.5: May all those others who hate us—those of evil intellect, evil intent, and evil resolves—not exist.
10.5: Rudra is so called because he cries out (*ru*), or because he runs about crying repeatedly (*rorūyamāna*), or from the root *rud* (to weep).
According to the *Kāṭhaka*, "Because he wept (*arodat*), that is the essence of Rudra's being Rudra."
10,5: "Because he wept (*arodat*), that is the *rudra*-ness of Rudra"—thus says the Hāridravika.
Regarding him, there is this [verse]:
10,6: "These songs for Rudra, who has a firm bow, for the god who possesses swift arrows and self-sovereignty..."
10.6: To the one who is unconquered, the victorious, the piercer, the wielder of sharp weapons—to him, bring [our praise] so that he may hear us!

10.6: Bring these songs to Rudra, the one with the firm bow, the swift-arrowed god, the possessor of food, the unconquered, the one who triumphs over others, the ordainer, the wielder of sharp weapons—bring them to him!
10.6: May he hear us!
10,6: *Tigma-tejas* [is derived] from the root *tij*, meaning "to exert" or "to stimulate.
10,6: *Āyudha* [is derived] from *ā-yodhana*, meaning "to fight.
10,6: Of this [word], there is another [verse].
10,7: "That lightning-flash of yours which, released from heaven, moves across the earth—may it spare us!
O you who are self-sustaining, may your thousand remedies protect us; do not harm our children or our descendants! 10,7:
That lightning-flash of yours which was released from heaven, from above the sky...
10,7: *Didyut* is derived from the root *dyat*, or *dyut*, or *dyot*. 10,7: It moves upon the earth (*kṣmayā carati*). 10,7: *Kṣmā* means the earth (*pṛthivī*).
She moves through its parts; she moves by means of it; or rather, she moves causing [them] to tremble.
May she spare us.
O thou who art well-attained, a thousand are thy words of healing.
10,7: O Mind, do not harm us among our sons and grandsons.
"Offspring" (*toka*) is derived from the root *tud* (to strike), and "descendant" (*tanaya*) is derived from the root *tan* (to extend). Agni is also called Rudra.
Regarding this, there is a verse: "O Jarābodha, perceive that for every people worthy of sacrifice; [offer] a beautiful hymn of praise to Rudra. (RV 7.93.6)

10,8: *Jarāstuti* is so called because it is a praise (*stuti*) derived from the root *jar*, which has the sense of praising. 10,8: "Be mindful of that," or alternatively, "by means of that, [be] the one who causes [us] to be mindful."
10,8: Understand that; 10,8: perform that;
10,8: for the sacrifice of every single human being.
10.8: A hymn worthy of being seen for Rudra. 10.8:

"Indra pierces *irā*," or "he gives *irā*," or "he bestows *irā*," or "he causes *irā* to flow," or "he sustains *irā*"; or [it is so called] because the drop (*indu*) flows, or because the drop rejoices, or because he kindles all beings. It is known from scripture: "Because they kindled him with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), that is the *indratva* (the state of Indra) of Indra. 10.8: "In that they kindled him with the vital breaths, that is the *indratva* of Indra. Thus it is understood.
10.8: "Because of this doing," says Āgrāyaṇa; "because of this seeing," says Aupamanyava;
or [it is derived] from the root *ind*, whose action is sovereignty.
10.8: [He is] the shatterer or the driver-away of enemies, and the one who causes the sacrificers to be honored.
Regarding him, there is this [verse]:
10.9: "You shattered [the mountain], you opened up the channels; you set free the obstructed floods."
10.9: "O Indra, when you split the great mountain and released the streams, you struck down the Dānava. 10.9: "You pierced the spring.
10.9: [The word] *utsa* is derived from *utsarati* (to flow out), or *utsadana* (sitting out), or *utsyandana* (flowing forth), or *unatti* (to moisten).
10,9: He opened his channels. 10,9: You held fast these watery oceans, these middle dwellings that were being obstructed.
10,9: The root *ram* has the sense of "binding."
10.9: Or [it concerns] the rite of dismissal.
10.9: "O Indra, when you opened the great mountain-cloud and released its streams, you struck down that Dānava who performs the act of giving.
Regarding this, there is another verse.
10.10: "He who, as soon as born, was the first wise god, who by his power (*kratu*) encompassed the gods;
at whose roar the two worlds trembled through the greatness of his manly might—he, O people, is Indra.
10.10: He who, even as he was being born, the swift and wise god, by his *kratu*—that is, by his action—encompassed, that is, he grasped, protected, or surpassed the gods.
10.10: By whose power heaven and earth were even struck with fear, through the greatness of his manly strength (*nṛmṇa*) and the magnitude of his might (*bala*).
10.10: "O people, he is Indra"—this is the joy of the seer who has perceived the truth, joined with a narrative.
10.10: Parjanya [is the deity] of the *tṛpa* hymn, whose beginning and end are reversed.
10,10: He is the one who satisfies the people;
10,10: or he is the supreme conqueror;
10,10: or he is the progenitor.
10,10: Or, he is the one who procures juices.
Regarding him, this [verse] occurs:
10,11: "He strikes down the trees and he strikes down the demons; the entire world fears him because of his great weapon."
10,11: Moreover, those who have committed no sin flee from the one possessing virile power, when Parjanya, thundering, strikes down the evildoers.
10,11: He shatters the trees; 10,11: and he shatters the *rakṣas* demons.
10,11: And all beings are afraid of him because of his great slaughter;
for his slaughter is indeed great.
Even one who is innocent flees in fear from him who possesses the power of rain, when Parjanya, thundering, strikes down evildoers and sinners.
10,11: Bṛhaspati is the protector or the guardian of the *bṛhat* (the Great).
Regarding him, there is this [verse]:
10,12: "They beheld the honey fastened by a stone, like a fish dwelling in shallow water."
10.12: Bṛhaspati, having split it apart with his roar, brought forth the honey as if one were to extract a cup from a tree.
10.12: They beheld the honey enveloped by a cloud full of lightning, like fish dwelling in shallow water.
10.12: He drew it out, just as one might take a cup from a tree.
10,12: Why "camasa"? 10,12: Because they sip (*camanti*) in it.
10,12: Bṛhaspati, having modified [it] with the sound of a cry (*virava*).
10.12: *Brahmaṇaspati* is either the Brahmin himself, or the protector, or the guardian.
Regarding him, there is this verse:
10.13: "Brahmaṇaspati pierced with his might that well whose mouth is stone, which has a flow of honey."

10,13: All those who behold the light of heaven have drunk from that very [fountain]; they have together poured much into the water-holding well. 10,13: That which possesses food, that which flows with streams, that which is unassailable—the stream of honey toward which Brahmanaspati has pressed with vigor and strength—that very [stream] all the rays, who behold the sun, drink; they pour much into it, into the water-holding, watery well. 10,14: The Lord of the Field.
10.14: *Kṣetra* [is derived] from the root *kṣi*, in the sense of the action of dwelling.
10.14: He is either its protector (*pātā*) or its guardian (*pālayitā*).
Regarding him, there is this [verse]:
10.15: "With the Lord of the Field, as with a benefactor, we conquer; nourishing cattle and horses, may he be gracious to us for such [a purpose]. 10.15:
"With the Lord of the Field, as with a well-disposed friend, we conquer; bring us cattle, horses, and nourishment."
May he be gracious to us in such a state;
whether by means of strength or by means of wealth.
The root *mṛḍ* has the sense of giving.
10.15: Or [it concerns] the rite of worship.
10.15: Regarding this, there is another verse:
10.16: "O Lord of the Field, pour out for us your honeyed wave, as a cow pours forth her milk."
10,16: "May the lords of Truth (*ṛta*) be gracious to us—[the waters] dripping with honey, well-purified like clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
10,16: "O Lord of the Field (*kṣetrapati*), milk for us a wave rich in honey, as a cow yields her milk.
10,16: "[The waters] dripping with honey, well-purified like water and clarified butter."
10.16: "May they protect us"—that is, may they be our guardians or may they be gracious to us.
The root *mṛḍayati* has the sense of showing compassion or the sense of honoring.
Now, when there is a common expression within the same verse, that constitutes *jāmi* (redundancy)—this is one view.

10.16: As in the case of "madhumantaṃ madhuścutam" (the honeyed, dripping honey). 10.16: Furthermore, when there is a repetition of the same expression within the same foot, that constitutes *jāmi* (redundancy), as in "hiranyarūpaḥ sa hiraṇyasaṃdṛk" (golden-formed, he who has a golden appearance).
10.16: "In whatever way there is a distinction, it becomes non-incestuous"—this is another [explanation].
10.16: "Like frogs from the water, like frogs from the water," as it were.
10.16: Vāstoṣpati.
10.16: Regarding the dwelling-place, the act of residing;
its protector or guardian—for him there is this [verse].
"O Vāstoṣpati, dispeller of disease, entering all forms,
be a kind friend to us.
O Vāstoṣpati, dispelling mental afflictions and entering all forms, be a very pleasant friend to us.
10,17: *Śeva* is a name for happiness (*sukha*).
10,17: It is derived from the root *śiṣ*.
10,17: The letter *va* is a name-former (*nāmakaraṇa*), an internal semi-vowel (*antastha*), characterized by an intermediate [nasal] resonance (*antara-upaliṅgin*), and its quality is manifested.
10.17: "It becomes auspicious" for him;
whatever form he desires, that very deity he becomes. There is also a Vedic verse (nigama) which says: "The Maghavan assumes every form."
10.17: Vācaspati. He is either the lord of speech or its protector. Regarding him, there is this [verse]:
"Come again, O Lord of Speech, with the divine mind;
O Lord of Wealth, free from disease, [place] my body within me alone"—this [verse] is explained by its recitation (*nigada*).
Apām Napāt, the Son of the Waters, has been explained.
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"He who shines unkindled within the waters, whom the sages praise during the sacrifices—
O Son of the Waters, grant us the honey-sweet waters, by which Indra was strengthened for heroic deeds."
10,19: He who shines without fuel, who blazes within the waters;
him whom the wise praise at the sacrifices—he, the Son of Waters, bestow the honeyed waters for the pressing.

10.19: "Those by which Indra increases for heroic power and manly deeds; Yama restrains the hundred"—of this [verse], there is this [stanza]: 10.19: "Those by which Indra increases for heroic power and manly deeds;
Yama restrains the hundred"—of this [verse], there is this [stanza].
10.20: "Honor with an oblation Yama, the King, the son of Vivasvat, the gathering place of men, who has departed along the great downward slopes, having spied out the path for many. 10.20:
*Pareyivāṃsam* means "one who has gone forth" or "one who has returned."
10,20: "Downward slope, upward slope, downward hollow"—the root *ava* functions as a verb meaning "to go. [He sees] one who is not looking along the path toward many [directions].
"10,20: Worship with an oblation Yama the King, the son of Vivasvat, the gathering place of people. By worshipping him, one accomplishes the ritual action.
10.20: Agni is also called Yama; these *ṛc* verses proclaim him accordingly. 10.21:
"Like an army let loose, he bears the arrow of the archer, with a blazing face."
10.21: Yama, once born, is the one who brings forth sacrifice; he is the lover of maidens and the husband of wives.
We approach him with our service, as cows reach their home when kindled. Thus are the *dvipadā* verses.
Like a released army, he bestows either fear or strength.
10.21: Like an archer’s shaft, he is of brilliant appearance, of powerful appearance, of glorious appearance, of great appearance, or of radiant appearance.
10.21: "Yama, indeed, was born together with Indra"—thus [it is said]. 10.21: There is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*) which says: "The two Yamas, here and there, are the mother."
10.21: Born like Yama, he is Yama to be born; the lover of maidens, the one who brings the maiden to maturity;
the husband of wives, the protector of women;
for they become preeminent through their connection with the sacrifice.

10.21: "Agni is your third husband"—thus also there is a *nigama* (Vedic citation). Thus also there is a *nigama*: "Go toward him, as one moves with the offering of cattle, and as one dwells with the offering of dwelling, and with the offering of herbs.
Just as cows reach their home, so may we reach him who is kindled and well-kindled with enjoyments.
10.21: Mitra protects those who have died.
Or, it is said that he runs about, bringing them together (*samminvāna*).
Or, [the name] is derived from the root *med* (to be fat).
Regarding him, there is this verse:
"Mitra, speaking, impels men; Mitra has supported both the earth and the sky.
Mitra gazes upon the people with unblinking eyes; offer an oblation rich in ghee unto Mitra."
