11,50: We invoke the swift chariot of the Maruts, the cloud worthy of being heard, upon which Rodasī dwells together with the Maruts, bearing waters that are most beautiful to behold. 12,1:
Now, therefore, follow the deities residing in heaven. Of these, the Aśvins are the first to arrive.
12.1: When the two Aśvins pervade everything—one with sap, the other with light;
[or] "the two Aśvins by means of horses," so says Aurṇavābha. Who, then, are the two Aśvins?
12.1: Some say they are heaven and earth;
some say they are day and night;
some say they are the sun and the moon.
12.1: "The two kings are performers of meritorious deeds," so say the historians. Of these two, the time after midnight follows the expansion of the state of light;
for the portion of darkness is the intermediate one, while the portion of light is the sun.
12,1: Regarding these two, there is this verse:
12,2: "O you two who move about among the dwellings, unclad like two rams—when did you two, O Aśvins, come hither to the gods? This [verse] is explained by its own recitation (*nigada*).

12,2: When these two [verses] belong to the same time and the same ritual action, and when they are nearly completed in their recitation, this half-verse occurs as a non-recitation [of the second]: "One is called Vāsātya; the other is your son, O Uṣas. 12,2: Of these two, there is this other [verse].
12,3: "Born here and there, they have lowed together with their stainless bodies and their own names.
One of you two is the victorious lord of the great sacrifice; the other, the fortunate son of heaven, is borne aloft.

Born both here and there, the two are praised with a body untainted by evil and with their own names. One of you two is *jisnu*, the impeller of great power, the intermediate one (the wind). The other, the fortunate son of heaven, is borne aloft—the Āditya (the Sun).
Regarding these two, there is this other [verse]:
"Awaken the two who yoke their chariot at dawn; let the Aśvins come hither for the drinking of this Soma."
12,4: Awaken the two Aśvins, who yoke their chariot at dawn;
let them come here to drink this Soma.
Regarding these two, there is this other verse:
12,5: "Sacrifice in the morning; urge on the Aśvins. There is no [sacrifice] in the evening that is not pleasing to the gods.
Moreover, another besides us sacrifices; each earlier sacrificer is more successful than the one after.
12,5: Sacrifice in the morning; send forth the two Aśvins.
12,5: There is no sacrifice to the gods in the evening; this is improper. Moreover, another besides us sacrifices; drive him away.
12.5: Each preceding sacrificer is more worthy of gain (*vanīyān*), most capable of winning over (*vanayitṛtama*).
The time for these two extends until sunrise; within that [time], other deities are also cast [into the fire].
*Uso* is derived from the root *vas* (or *vaś*), which has the sense of desiring or longing.
12.5: *Ucchati* [the Dawn] shines forth; the other [verse] belongs to the midday pressing.
Regarding that [Dawn], there is this [verse]:
"O possessor of plenty, bring to us that wonderful wealth of yours."
12.5: "By which we may support both our children and our grandchildren.
12.6: O Dawn, bring to us that wonderful, praiseworthy, and magnificent wealth, O you who abound in food, by which we may sustain both sons and grandsons.
Regarding this, there is another verse:
12,7: "These very dawns have made their banner; they have recognized the light in the eastern half of the mid-region.
Like bold warriors preparing their weapons, the ruddy cows, the mothers, come forth.
12,7: These dawns have made that banner, a sign of intelligence.
12,7: The plural number may be used for the sake of honoring even a single one.
12,7: In the eastern half, they anoint themselves with the splendor of the intermediate world;
like bold warriors preparing their weapons, they act with courage.
12.7: *nir* occurs in place of this [prefix] *sam*. 12.7:
There is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*) which says: "I go to their appointed place, like a wanton woman. 12.7: They return from the going of the cattle.
12.7: Aruṣī from the luminous realm; Mātariśvan’s mother, the fashioner; Sūryā, the wife of Sūrya.
12.7: This very [verse] is the most appropriate for the time of departure.
Regarding it, there is this [verse]:
12.8: "The *kiṃśuka* tree, the *śalmali*, all-formed, golden-colored, well-constructed, with beautiful wheels."
12,8: "Ascend to the world of immortality, O Sūryā; prepare a pleasant bridal procession for your husband.
12,8: "It is well-shining, auspicious, pure, and of every form.
12,8: Or rather, it may have the sense of a comparison, as in "like the *kiṃśuka* tree upon the *śalmali*."
12,8: The *kiṃśuka* tree is so called because it makes the action of shining manifest. 12,8: The *śalmali* tree is "well-reed" (*suśara*), or rather, it possesses reeds (*śaravat*).
12,8: O Sūrya, ascend to the world of immortality, [the realm] of water.
12.8: "Make the bridegroom happy.
12.8: And there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "Savitar gave Sūryā to Soma, O King, or to Prajāpati.
12.8: Vṛṣākapāyī is the wife of Vṛṣākapi.
12.8: This very [rite] is the most appropriate for the time when [the husband] has been released [from his vows].
Regarding it, there is this [verse]:
"O wealthy Vṛṣākapāyī, you who have good sons and indeed a good daughter-in-law..."
12.8: "O Indra, eat the oxen; [eat] the dear oblation that brings about whatever is desired. O Indra, you are superior to all. 12.9:
"The wife of Vṛṣākapi is wealthy, possessing good sons, through her middle [voice]; she is well-nourished through the midday speech. 12.9:
"'Snuṣā' means 'one who sits well,' or 'one who acquires well,' or 'she acquires that which is good offspring.'"
12,9: Indra has asked these middle dwellings for his bulls (*ukṣan*).
12,9: *Ukṣan* [is derived] from the root *ukṣ*, meaning "to grow" (*vṛddhi-karman*). 12,9: Or alternatively, it means "they sprinkle with water."
12,9: Make dear the oblation that brings happiness, the oblation that produces well-being. 12,9:
O Indra, whoever is supreme over all, him we call this Āditya. 12,9:
*Saraṇyū*s from the act of moving swiftly.

Regarding her, there is this verse: "12.9: They concealed the immortal one from mortals; having made her of similar form, they gave her to Vivasvat. And she brought forth the two Aśvins when that occurred;
Saranyū abandoned the two pairs of twins. 12.10: "They concealed the immortal one from mortals; having made her of similar form, they gave her to Vivasvat.
And she brought forth the two Aśvins when that occurred; Saranyū abandoned the two pairs of twins."
They concealed the immortal [goddess] from mortals;
having made her of similar appearance, they gave her to Vivasvat.
She bore the two Aśvins when that [immortal one] was there; Saraṇyū abandoned the two twins.
"The middle one and the one belonging to the middle," so say the etymologists (*nairuktāḥ*).
"Yama and Yamī," so say the historians (*aitihāsikāḥ*). Regarding this, they relate the following historical narrative (*itihāsa*): [text continues]

12.10: Tvaṣṭṛ’s wife, Saraṇyū, gave birth to the twin Yamas from Vivasvat Āditya. Having substituted another woman of similar appearance (Savarṇā), she assumed the form of a mare and fled. Vivasvat Āditya, assuming the very form of a horse, pursued her and united with her.
12.10: From that, the Aśvins were born;
from Svarṇā, Manu was born.
Regarding this, there is this verse of praise.
12,11: “Tvaṣṭṛ prepares the bridal procession for his daughter,” so saying, this entire world assembles.
As she is being led away, Yama’s mother, the great wife of Vivasvat, vanished.
“Tvaṣṭṛ prepares the conveyance for his daughter,” so saying, this entire world assembles.
12,11: And all these beings come together here.
Yama’s mother, being carried away, vanished as the great wife of Vivasvat.
Night, belonging to the Āditya, disappears at the rising of the Āditya.
12.12: Savitṛ has been explained.
His time is when the sky becomes free from darkness and filled with rays.
Of him, there is this [verse]:
12.13: "The Seer puts on all forms; he has brought forth what is auspicious for the biped and the quadruped.
Savitṛ, the one to be chosen, has looked upon the vault of heaven; he shines following the departure of the Dawn.
This [verse] belongs to him.
The wise man puts on all forms of wisdom;
he becomes a seer (*kavi*), one who has transcendent vision—either from the root *kav* (to see) or *kav* (to shine). He brings forth what is auspicious for both the bipeds and the quadrupeds.
12,13: Savitṛ, the one to be chosen, has intended to ascend to heaven;
he shines forth following the departure of the Dawn. 12,13:
It is known from the enumeration of sacrificial animals that "the Adhorāma belongs to Savitṛ."
12,13: "On account of what similarity?
12,13: "Because at that time there was darkness below; on account of this similarity. 12,13: "Rāma is below, Kṛṣṇa is below—on account of what similarity?"
12,13: "Having piled the fire-altar, one should not approach a *rāmā*. "A *rāmā* is for pleasure, not for dharma. 12,13:
[She is] of the dark class (*kṛṣṇa-jātīyā*) because of this commonality. 12,13: It is known from the enumeration of sacrificial animals that "the cock belongs to Savitṛ."
12,13: On account of what commonality? 12,13: Having bypassed the mention of time.
12,13: First is the imitation of the sound of a cock, followed by that of a *vacas*.
12,13: Bhaga has been explained. 12,13: His time is prior to the upward movement [of the sun]. 12,13: Regarding him, there is this [verse]:
"May we invoke at dawn the victorious, formidable Bhaga, the son of Aditi, who is the ordainer of all.
Thinking even of him as one who is weak, or even as one who is swift, or even as a king, the man says, 'Bhaga has granted me my portion.
"May we invoke at dawn the victorious, formidable Bhaga, the son of Aditi, who is the sustainer of everything."

Even the one who considers himself weak, the seeker of aid, the poor man—even the powerful one (the word *tura* being a name for Yama, derived either from *tṛ*, "to cross over," or *tvar*, "to hasten";
Yama is so called because he moves with swift speed).
Even a king says of him: "May I partake of Bhaga."
"‘Bhaga is blind,’ they say, for he is not seen because he has not emerged;
‘He struck out his eyes with the *prāśitra*’—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Or it is also known: ‘Bhaga goes among the people.’"
12,14: [The sun] goes to the people at sunrise.
12,14: *Sūrya* is derived from the root *sar* (to move), or *suv* (to impel), or *svīry* (to possess power).
12,14: Regarding him, there is this verse:
12,15: "They bear aloft that Jātavedas, the god Sūrya, as a banner for all to see. 12,15:
They bear up that Jātavedas, Sūrya, as rays—the banner of all beings—for the purpose of seeing.
12,15: Who else but Āditya would have spoken thus?
12,15: Of him there is this other [verse]:
12,16: "The brilliant face of the gods has risen—the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni."

12,16: The Sun has filled heaven, earth, and the intermediate space; he is the soul of all that moves and stands. 12,16: The adorable countenance of the gods has risen, the manifestation of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni.
12.16: By his greatness, he filled the heaven and earth and the intermediate space. He is the sun, the soul of all that moves and all that is stationary.
Furthermore, because he nourishes the growth of the rays, he becomes Pūṣan.
Regarding him, there is this [verse]:
"Thy one part is bright, thy other part is worthy of sacrifice; thou art like the sky with its two days of different forms.
For thou, O self-dependent one, dost master all wondrous powers. O Pūṣan, may thy bounty here be auspicious!"
12,17: One part of you is bright, another is red; one part is worthy of sacrifice, another is fit for worship.
12,17: Your two days have different forms; your work is like the sky. 12,17: And you are like heaven itself.
12,17: May all forms of wisdom be at hand for you.
O Pūṣan, may your gift be here like a vessel.
Regarding this, there is another verse:
12,18: "With eloquence, he has approached the protector of every path, impelled by desire;
may Pūṣan grant us wealth with bright treasures; may he bring each prayer to fulfillment. 12,18:
"The lord of every path, impelled by speech and by desire, has approached the *arka*; or rather, 'he has approached the *arka*' means 'he has reached the *arka*.'"
12.18: May he grant us desirable and foremost riches;
may Pūṣan accomplish every task for us. Thus it is said.
Now, when one is *visita*, then one becomes Viṣṇu.
12.18: Viṣṇu is so called because he enters (*viśati*) or because he pervades (*vy-aśnute*).
12.18: Regarding him, there is this [verse]:
12.19: "Viṣṇu strode across this [universe]; in three places he established his step; his footstep is gathered in the dust."
Whatever this is, Viṣṇu strides over it;
he places his foot in three ways—
for the sake of a threefold existence— upon the earth, in the intermediate space, and in heaven, so says Śākapūṇi.
12.19: Aurṇavābha says that [the footprint] is on the ascent, at Viṣṇu’s step, and at the head of Gaya.

12.19: "His footprint is completely submerged in the dust; it is not seen even in the expanse of the sky. 12.19: Or rather, it may be for the sake of comparison: "His footprint is as if completely submerged in dust; it is not seen."

12,19: They are called *pāṃsupāda* either because they are produced from dust and feet (*pāṃsu-pādaiḥ sūyante*), or because they lie fallen (*pannāḥ śerate*), or because they are to be crushed (*piṃśanīyā bhavanti*).
12,20: *Viśvānara* has been explained.
This is its occurrence in a verse addressed to Indra (*aindrī ṛc*).
"Of Viśvānara, the lord of the forest-tree, of unbending power;
with the movements and for the protection of the people, I call upon the chariots.

I invoke Indra at this sacrifice with the movements, desires, paths, or protections of Viśvānara—the Āditya—of unbending power, of great strength, and for the sake of the movements, paths, or protections of the people, that is, of human beings, as well as by way of the roads of the chariots.
12,21: Varuṇa has been explained.
This is his [hymn]:
12,22: "O Purifier, with that eye wherewith you look upon the people as they stir..."
12,22: "O Varuṇa, you see.
12,22: *Bhuranyu* is a name for "swift.
12,22: The swift bird leads one along the vast path.
12,22: The bringer even of the heavenly world;
12,22: reaching that [world], he is full of longing;
12,22: by this account of the Purifier (Pāvaka).
12.22: "Moving among the people," 12.22: "you, O Varuṇa, behold," 12.22: "that of yours we praise"—this is the completion of the sentence.
12.22: Or rather, [it is recited] on the subsequent [verse].

12.23: "O Purifier, with that eye wherewith you look upon the people as they stir about, O Varuṇa, [with that do you look upon us]. "You traverse the sky, spreading it wide, measuring out the nights."

12.23: Beholding the births, O Sūrya, you pervade the sky and the broad mid-air; measuring out the great world along with the days and the nights, O Sūrya, you behold all beings that have been born—or rather, [you behold] the former.

12.24: "O Purifier, with that eye wherewith you look upon the people as they stir about, O Varuṇa, you behold [all]. "You face the hosts of the gods; you face the human beings; you face all so that the light may be seen."
12.24: "Thou risest toward all this; 12.24: 'Thou art called the light facing toward this'; 12.24: 'Thou beholdest all this facing toward it.'"
Or rather, on this very [verse]:
"O Purifier, with that chest by which you look upon the people as they stir,
O Varuṇa."
12.25: With that, O Keśin, you look down upon us people. "Keśin" means one who possesses hair; here, "hair" refers to the rays, and he becomes possessed of them by means of those [rays].
12.25: [It is so called] because of illuminating or making manifest.
Regarding this, there is this verse:
12.26: "The long-haired one bears Agni; the long-haired one bears poison; the long-haired one bears the two worlds."

12,26: "The long-haired one (keśī) is the all-light for seeing; the long-haired one is called this light. 12,26: The long-haired one [perceives] both fire and water. 12,26: "Water" (viṣ) is a name for water, derived from the root *snā* meaning "to purify," preceded by the prefix *vi*.
12.26: Or [the suffix *kvin* is applied] after the root *sac*, preceded by *vi*.
12.26: And he supports heaven and earth. 12.26: The long-haired one (*keśin*) gazes upon all this, this entire universe.
12,26: "The one with hair (keśī) is called this light," he says, referring to the sun. Furthermore, these other two lights are also called "hairy" (keśinī):
fire by means of smoke, and the intermediate [air] by means of dust.

12,26: This verse belongs to them in common: 12,27: "Three long-haired ones appear in due season; one of them shears during the year. One of them gazes upon the universe with his powers; the speed of one is seen, but not his form."
12,27: Three long-haired ones appear in due season; at every appointed time they look abroad.
(12,26) 12,27: "In the year one of them shaves [the earth]"; thus Agni consumes the earth with fire.
12.27: The Sun beholds everything through its actions; the path of the One is seen, but not the form of the Middle One. 12.27: Not the form of the Middle One. (12.27)
12.27: Now, when he goes forth shaking [the world] with his rays, he becomes Vṛṣākapi, the "Shaker of the Bull.
12.28: Of him, this [verse] shines:
"Come back again, O Vṛṣākapi; let us two arrange for our well-being."

12,28: "O Indra, you who are the destroyer of sleep, you go to your setting by that path; yet you are superior to all. 12,28: "Come back again, O Vṛṣākapi! Let us two arrange our well-performed deeds together. 12,28: "The destroyer of sleep—you destroy dreams with the rising of the sun; thus you go to your setting by that path once more."
12.28: He who is superior to all, O Indra—that Āditya we here speak of.
12.28: Yama has been explained.
12.28: Of him, this [verse] occurs.
"On the well-leafed tree where Yama drinks together with the gods—
there our father, the lord of the people, looks back upon us who have passed away.
On that well-leafed tree, in that place, or in the dwelling of Vṛtra.
Alternatively, it may be used in the sense of a comparison, as in "like a tree with beautiful foliage" (*vṛkṣa iva supalāśa iti*).
A tree (*vṛkṣa*) is so called from the act of cutting (*vraścana*); foliage (*palāśa*) is so called from the act of shining forth or spreading (*palāśana*).
Yama comes together with the gods; the Āditya [comes] with his rays.
There, may the Protector or the Guardian of all desire our ancestors.
[May] Aja Ekapād [grant this].
12.29: *Ajana* means "one-footed. Alternatively, it is so called because he protects with one foot;
or alternatively, because he drinks with one foot.
12,29: Or, "one foot of it remains.
There is also a Vedic citation (nigama) stating, "He does not lift up one foot.
This is its specific occurrence in a verse dedicated to the Viśvedevas.

12.30: "The daughter of the thunderbolt, born of the one-footed [heaven], the supporter of heaven, the river, and the waters of the ocean—may all the gods hear my words, along with Sarasvatī, together with inspired thoughts and wisdom.
12.30: The *pavi* becomes the barb when it pierces the body.
12.30: Likewise, the weapon is the *pavīra*;
Indra, possessing that, is *pavīravān*.
There is also a Vedic citation (*nigama*) which says: "The one possessing the *pavīra* has transcended."

12.30: Let the speech of that deity, Pāvīravī; and let the divine speech Pāvīravī, the thundering sound that brings forth another voice; and Aja Ekapād, the sustainer of heaven, Sindhu, the waters of the ocean, and all the gods together with Sarasvatī and Purandhi—let them hear these words uttered with praise, joined with prayers and ritual acts. Thus it is said.
12.30: *Pṛthivī* (the earth) has been explained.
This is its occurrence in a verse addressed to Indra and Agni:
12.31: "O Indra and Agni, whether you are in the highest earth, in the middle one, or even in the lowest..."
12,31: "Therefore, O you two stallions, come hither; then drink of the pressed soma"—this [verse] is explained by its own recitation (*nigada*). 12,31: *Samudra* has been explained.
12,31: This is its occurrence in a *pāvamānī* verse.
12,32: "The purifiers sit around the speech; their ancient father protects their vow. Varuṇa has hidden himself within the great ocean; the wise have been able to grasp him in his foundations.
12,32: The divine hosts of the mid-region, possessing the purifier and possessing rays, sit around the speech of the mid-region.
12.32: Their middle father, ancient and primeval, protects his vow and his work.
Varuṇa, the great one, conceals [the world] within the ocean; then the wise are able to undertake the beginning of their work upon the supporting waters. Aja Ekapād has been explained.
12.32: Pṛthivī has been explained;
Samudra has been explained.
This is their occurrence in another ṛc that has many deities.
12,33: "And may Ahibudhnya hear us, and Aja Ekapād, the Earth, and the Ocean;
may all the gods who increase Truth, being invoked, and the hymns praised by sages, protect us.

Furthermore: May Ahibudhnya hear us, and Aja Ekapād, the Earth, and the Ocean, and all the gods who increase Truth or increase the sacrifice; and may the hymns, being invoked with mantras and praised, and the mantras recited by sages—that is, those recited by the wise—protect us.
12,33: [The word] *dadhyam* means "meditation directed inward" (*pratyakto dhyānam*), or "in which meditation is directed inward" (*pratyaktaṃ dhyānam asmin*).
12,33: *Atharvan* has been explained. 12,33: *Manu* [is so called] from the act of thinking (*mananāt*).
12,33: This insertion occurs for them in a verse addressed to Indra (aindrī ṛc).

12,34: "The prayer which Atharvan, the father of Manu, stretched out with devotion—unto that [prayer] the ancient Brahman-formulas and the hymns of praise met together; they sang in accordance with his self-sovereignty."

12,34: That which Atharvan and Manu, the father of men, and Dadhyañc contemplated as their mental vision—may the sacred hymns, the ritual acts, and the ancient praises of Indra converge upon that. Singing your songs, you shall attain sovereign rule.
12,35: Now, therefore, follow the divine hosts dwelling in heaven. Of these, the Ādityas are the first to arrive.
12,35: The Ādityas have been explained.
This is their [verse]:
12,36: "These songs, dripping with clarity, I offer eternally with the ladle to the Ādityas, the kings."
12.36: May Mitra, Aryaman, Bhaga, the many-born Varuṇa, Dakṣa, and Aṃśa hear us.

12.36: With a ladle dripping with ghee—whether as those that flow with ghee, those that pour forth ghee, those that stream with ghee, or those that abound in ghee—I offer these oblations for a long time to the Ādityas, for long life, or for the sake of the kings.
12.36: May Mita, Aryaman, Bhaga, the many-born Dhātṛ, Dakṣa, Varuṇa, and Aṃśa hear these songs of ours.
12.36: *Aṃśa* has been explained by means of *aṃśu*.
12.36: The Seven Seers (*saptarṣayaḥ*) have been explained.
Regarding them, there is this [verse]:

12,37: "Seven seers are established within the body; seven guard it always with vigilance. Seven waters have gone to the world of the sleeper; there two gods remain wakeful, sleepless, and ever-present at the sacrifice.
12,37: The seven seers established in the body are the rays in the sun.
12.37: Seven guard [the world] perpetually with vigilance; for a year they remain vigilant.
These same seven are the attainers who go to their own world when the sun has set.
Here, Vāyu and Āditya are the two gods who are wakeful, sleepless, and seated at the sacrificial session (*sattra*).
12.37: Thus with reference to the deities. Now with reference to the self: the seven seers are established within the body; together with the senses, knowledge is the seventh within the self.
12,37: Seven guard the body constantly and vigilantly; they remain watchful over it. 12,37:
These seven sufferings indeed go to the world of sleep, to the self that has set. 12,37:
Here, two gods remain wakeful and sleepless, ever-seated at the sacrificial session—the wise self (*prājña-ātman*) and the radiant self (*taijasa*).
12,37: Thus he declares the course of the self.
12,37: Of these, there is this other [verse]:
12,38: "The ladle with its opening below and its base above, in which glory of every form is deposited."
12,38: Here sit together the seven seers who were the guardians of this great one.
12,38: It is a ladle with a horizontal opening, an upward-binding, or an upward-awakening, 12,38: in which glory is deposited in every form.
12,38: Here sit the seven seers together with the rays of the sun, who have become the guardians of this great [being]; thus far concerning the deity.
12,38: Now concerning the self (adhyātma).
It is a ladle with a horizontal opening, its binding above and its perception above—or rather, it is the consciousness directed upwards.

food and drink constitute the eighth.
14.5: This person consists of all things and is fashioned as possessing all knowledge. 14.6: Whatever he conforms to, that he becomes. If he conforms to dharma, he becomes a god.
14,6: If one pursues knowledge, one becomes immortal; if one pursues desire, one falls away. He would enter this womb.
14,6: This is the view held here:
phlegm arises from semen;
from phlegm comes chyle.

14.6: From plasma comes blood; from blood, flesh; from flesh, fat; from fat, sinews; from sinews, bones; from bones, marrow; from marrow, semen. 14.6: This semen, when emitted into the womb, becomes a person.
When there is an excess of semen, one becomes male; when there is an excess of blood, one becomes female.

14,6: By two [equal] [quantities], one becomes a neuter. 14,6: By an unequal [quantity of] semen, one becomes Yama (a twin). This occurs through the union of semen and blood, and through the union of the mother and father.
14.6: How is this body completely restrained?
It becomes gentle;
having remained for one night, it becomes a *kalala*.
14.6: After five nights, the bubble-like stage (*budbuda*) [forms];
after seven nights, the fleshy mass (*peśī*);
after fourteen nights, the solid lump (*ghana*).
14.6: After twenty-five nights, it becomes a solid mass (*ghana*).
After one month, it becomes firm (*kathina*).
Within two months, the head is fully formed.
In the third month, the formation of the neck is indicated; in the fourth month, the formation of the skin is indicated.
In the fifth month, the formation of the nails and hair is indicated. In the sixth month, the mouth, nose, and eyes [are formed].
In the sixth month, the sense of hearing arises;
in the seventh, he becomes capable of movement; in the eighth, he determines through the intellect;
in the ninth, all his limbs become fully developed.
14.6: "I have died and been born again; having been born, I have died again.
Indeed, thousands of various wombs have been inhabited by me.
Various kinds of food have been eaten, and many kinds of breasts have been sucked."

14.6: "One has seen various mothers and fathers, as well as friends; likewise, a living being, afflicted and joined [to suffering], should practice Sāṃkhya and Yoga, or [meditate upon] the twenty-fifth principle, the Puruṣa. Thus [it is said].
14.6: Then, in the tenth month, it is born;
and once born, touched by the wind, it does not remember birth, death, and so forth;
and at the end, there is the good and evil karma—this is the measure of the body.
14.7: There are one hundred and eight joints. 14.7: The head consists of eight skull-bones.
14.7: There are sixteen leaf-like portions of the omentum.
There are nine hundred sinews;

there are seven hundred vital points (*marman*) in a person; there are thirty-five million hairs; the heart consists of eight cranial plates; the tongue consists of twelve cranial plates; and the two testicles are like two well-feathered birds.
14.7: Likewise, the genitals, anus, and rectum—why are these [the seats of] urine and feces? Because they are moistened by food and drink.
14.7: "Beings whose karma has not been exhausted are born from one another.
14.7: "Knowledge and karma, as well as prior cognition, accompany him.

14.7: "Sunk in the great darkness of ignorance, overwhelmed by the pairs of opposites consisting of old age, death, hunger, thirst, sorrow, anger, greed, delusion, pride, fear, envy, joy, despondency, jealousy, and malice, he is liberated from this state of the swift transformations of existence."

14.7: From this body, which is like a great vessel of evil, having departed in a mere moment, having passed beyond its natural state, and having fashioned a luminous body (*taijasa-śarīra*) corresponding to the fruit of its karma, it experiences that fruit; upon the exhaustion of that karma, it returns again to this world.
14.8: Now, those who resort to violence, abandoning knowledge, and perform great austerities for a long time, or perform the rites prescribed in the Veda—they pass into smoke.
From smoke they go to night; from night, to the waning fortnight.

From the waning fortnight one goes to the southern course; from the southern course to the world of the ancestors; from the world of the ancestors to the moon; from the moon to the wind; from the wind to rain; and from rain to plants. Having become this, upon the exhaustion of that [merit], one returns once again to this very world.

14.9: Now, those who, having abandoned violence and resorted to knowledge, perform great austerities, or perform actions prescribed by knowledge—they pass into the light (*arcis*). From the light, they go to the day; from the day, to the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight, to the six months of the northern course of the sun; from the northern course, to the world of the gods (*devaloka*); from the world of the gods, to the sun; from the sun, to lightning; and from lightning, they reach the mind-born (*mānasa*) state.
Having become mind-born persons, they pass into the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*). They do not return again.
14,9: There are those remaining who are like thorns on a staff, who do not understand this.
Therefore, this must be understood.
Moreover, it is also said:
14.10: "You do not know him who generated these [beings]; something else has come between you.
Enveloped by mist and idle chatter, well-satisfied, they go about reciting hymns.
14.10: The wise do not know him whom those who truly know declare to be the Imperishable Lord of Prayer (Brahmaṇaspati).
14,10: "One thing belongs to you, another to them; there was a difference between them. 14,10:
"Enveloped by mist, by darkness, and by delusion, these seekers of life, who feed on the breath of others and rule over the sacrificial pot, wander along the paths when they go toward the sun.
14,10: "The ignorant proclaim [themselves] to be knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*)."
14.10: Now, O wise ones, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) prepares himself.
Through his austerity, he attains vigilance; then he becomes one who is to be attained. By means of that, he should desire [the goal] without interruption.
One should desire friendship with him, for he is the best of friends; he understands the past, the present, and the future.
Why is he called the "Knower" (Jñātṛ)? Because of birth (jāyateḥ).
14,10: Why "friend" (*sakhi*)? From the root *sakhyati*. 14,10: They lie together with the sense organs.
Or, it is because the Great Elements, together with the sense organs, cause Prajñā to perform action.
14,10: Water is its foundation;
its nature is ethical conduct and tranquility, and it is Brahman. Thus, having become one with Brahman, it remains as a mere witness, liberated from the bonds created by ignorance.
14,10: Now, we shall first enumerate the names of the elements belonging to the Great Self.
14,11: Haṃsa.
14,11: Gharma.
14,11: Sacrifice;
14,11: The longing one/the cloud; 14,11: The worm.
14,11: The ground;
14,11: The pervasive lord;
14,11: The sovereign master.
14,11: Śambhu;
14,11: Rābhu;
14,11: Vardhakarmā.
14,11: Bhūta;
14,11: Bhuvana.
14,11: The future;
14,11: the waters;
14,11: the great.
14,11: the sky;
14,11: glory;
14,11: greatness.
14,11: Golden-hued;
14,11: Recollected; 14,11: Well-recalled.
14,11: satīkam / 14,11: satīnam / 14,11: gahanam /
14,11: Deep; 14,11: Cavernous;
14,11: food; 14,11: oblation;
14,11: the seat; 14,11: the cosmic order; 14,11: the womb.
14,11: The womb of cosmic order; 14,11: truth; 14,11: water.
14,11: Oblation; 14,11: Wealth;
14,11: Truth.
14,11: Imperishable.
14,11: Barhis;
14,11: Nāman;
14,11: Sarpis.
14,11: The waters; 14,11: the purifier; 14,11: the immortal.
14,11: The sun;
14,11: the creations; 14,11: Śambara.
14,11: the atmosphere; 14,11: the sky; 14,11: the void.
14,11: The lightning-bolt; 14,11: The desert; 14,11: The intermediate space.
14,11: Space; 14,11: Water; 14,11: Earth.
14,11: Bhūḥ / 14,11: Svayambhūḥ / 14,11: Adhvan /
14,11: Puskara;
14,11: Sagara; 14,11: Samudra.
14,11: Austerity;
14,11: Splendor; 14,11: The Ocean.
14,11: the ocean; 14,11: the navel; 14,11: the udder.
14,11: A tree;
14,11: Brahman. 14,11: The most excellent.
14,11: The swan;
14,11: the self;
14,11: they become.
14,11: They strike; 14,11: the path;
14,11: that which is outside.
14.11: [The word] *śarīrāṇi* [is used]; 14.11:
[the word] *avyayaṃśca* [is used] in the *saṃskṛta* [language];
14.11: [the word] *yajñaḥ*.
14,11: It becomes the self (ātman). When they extend it [the sacrifice], then these hymns (sūktas) and these verses (ṛcs) proclaim this great self after it.
"Soma flows clear, the progenitor of prayers, the progenitor of heaven, the progenitor of earth;
the progenitor of Agni, the progenitor of Sūrya, the progenitor of Indra, and the progenitor of Viṣṇu.
Soma flows clear, the generator of prayers, the generator of heaven, the generator of earth, the generator of Agni, the generator of Sūrya, the generator of Indra, and the generator of Viṣṇu.
14,12: Soma flows clear.
14,12: Soma is the Sun;
he is the progenitor of inspirations (*matīnām*)—that is, of the rays of the sun whose function is illumination—and of the rays of the sun whose function is shining in heaven (*divaḥ*).
14.12: Of the solar rays whose function is the expansion of the earth; 14.12:
of the solar rays whose function is the movement of fire; 14.12:
of the solar rays whose function is the appropriation by the sun.

14,12: Of the solar rays that perform the acts of sovereignty belonging to Indra; 14,12: of the solar rays that perform the acts of pervasion belonging to Viṣṇu. Thus with reference to the deities (adhidaivata).
14.12: Now, with respect to the self (*adhyātma*).
The meaning is that Soma is also the progenitor of the sense organs from this very [source].
Or rather, he is the Self manifested through all his powers (*vibhūti*).
14,12: Thus he declares his own course.

14,13: "Brahmā among the gods, the pathfinder for the poets, the seer among the sages, the buffalo among wild beasts, the hawk among vultures, the axe among the forests—Soma, chanting, passes beyond the filter."
"Brahmā of the gods.
For he is indeed the Brahmā of the gods—of those whose function is to play (devana)—that is, of the rays of the sun. "The path-finder of the seers."
"For he knows the station of the poets who are striving to be poets, [the station] of the rays of the sun;
he is the seer among the inspired ones.
For he becomes the seer of the inspired ones, of the rays of the sun whose activity is all-pervading.
14.13: "The buffalo among wild animals.
For he is indeed the greatest among wild animals, those whose function is seeking, namely the rays of the sun.
14.13: "The hawk among vultures."

14.13: The Āditya is a *śyena* (hawk/eagle), from the root *śyai*, which means "to go. 14.13: The Āditya is a *gṛdhra* (vulture), from the root *gṛdh*, which means "to stand still," because he stands upon this [world].
"14,13: 'The axe of the woods'—for this Āditya himself performs his own actions among the woods, that is, among the rays of the sun which perform the act of gathering. 14,13:
'Soma goes across the filter, chanting.'"
14.13: For he, being praised, transcends the rays, which are the means of purification.
14.13: He alone is all this imperishable.
Thus with respect to the divine.
14.13: Now with reference to the self: "The Brahman among the gods.
This one also becomes the Brahman among the gods—the senses—whose function is that of playing (*devana*).
"14,13: *padavīḥ kavīnām* (the pathfinder of the seers).
This one also knows the station (*pada*) of the seers who act as seers, that is, of the senses.
14,13: *ṛṣir viprāṇām* (the seer among the inspired poets)."

14.13: This [bull] is also the seer of the senses whose function is non-destruction, for they are called "vipras" (the wise). "The buffalo among wild animals"—this [bull] is also great among the wild animals, for the senses have the function of seeking (*mārgana*).
14.13: "The hawk among vultures.

14.13: He becomes the self of the hawk (*śyena*), from the root *śyai*, meaning the act of knowing. 14.13: The senses are the vultures (*gṛdhra*), from the root *gṛdh*, meaning the act of knowing, because they abide in him.
"14,13: 'The axe of the woods'—this [Soma] himself also places his own actions within himself, namely the actions of 'winning' (*vanana*) the woods, that is, the senses. 14,13:
'Soma, singing, passes through the filter.'"
14.13: This [sacrifice] also is a purifier that transcends the senses;
being praised, it alone experiences all this and declares the course of the Self.

14,14: "The bearer (vahni) utters forth three voices: the thought of the Ṛta, the inspired wisdom of the Brahman. Like cows seeking their master, they go toward the Lord of Cows; like lowing thoughts, the prayers go toward Soma. (ṚV 10.97.34). 14,14: The bearer (vahni) is the Āditya.
14,14: He impels the threefold speech: the *ṛc*s, the *yajus* formulas, and the *sāman* chants;
the deeds of *ṛta*, of the Āditya, which are the thoughts of Brahman.
This very one is all this imperishable (*akṣara*).
14.14: Thus with reference to the deities. Now with reference to the self: the self becomes the fire.
14,14: He impels, he sets in motion, the sixfold speech of those possessed of knowledge, understanding, and intelligence;
[he impels] the actions of the Self of Truth (Ṛta), the thoughts of Brahman.
This very one experiences all this.
14,14: He declares his own course.
14,15: "The cows, the milch-kine, lowing toward Soma; the sages, questioning with their hymns, [seek] Soma.
The pressed Soma is purified while being anointed; to Soma the *ṛk*-verses and the *triṣṭubh*s join together" (ṚV 9.97.35).
14,15: Just as these cows, the milch-cows, or rather the rays, lowing—that is, desiring—go toward Soma, who is the Āditya;
even so do the sages, the rays, questioning with their thoughts and desiring, go toward Soma, who is the Āditya.
Even so is Soma purified when pressed and being anointed.
14,15: The *ṛks* and the *triṣṭubhs* sing this very [song] together. Therefore, in this [breath], they become one with the Āditya. Thus far with respect to the deities (*adhidaivata*).
14,15: Now, with reference to the self (*adhyātma*). These very cows, the milch-cows—the senses—going toward Soma, desiring him, enter into the self.
In this very same way, the inspired poets (*vipra*), the senses, questioning Soma with their thoughts and desiring him, enter into the self.
In this very way, the pressed Soma is purified while being anointed.
This very self and the seven seers sing praises together.
These [elements] become one within this self.
14,15: Thus he declares his own course.
14,16: "The ocean has moved forward in the first ordinance, generating progeny, the king of the world;
the bull upon the sheep-wool filter, on its summit, Soma, the pressed drop, has grown great" (ṚV 9.97.40).
14.16: The Sun has transcended the ocean into the highest firmament through his work of raining; as King of the world, he brings forth all creatures, the King of all.
14.16: The bull, upon the sheep’s back, the drop of Soma, being pressed, has increased greatly within the filter.
Thus with reference to the deities.

Now, with reference to the self: The ocean-like Self has transcended into the supreme expanse, generating creatures through knowledge and action, the king of the world, the king of all. The bull, upon the sheep’s back in the filter, Soma, the pressed drop, has increased greatly.
14,16: Thus he declares his own course.
14,17: "That Soma, the Great One, the Buffalo, performed [this deed] when, as the embryo of the waters, he chose the gods;
as the purifying Indu, he bestowed vigor upon Indra, and generated light in the sun" (ṚV 9.97.41).
14,17: That great deed the mighty Soma performed, when as the embryo of the waters he chose [the gods].
He bestowed sovereign lordship over the gods upon Indra; as the purifying one, he generated vigor in the sun and light, he, the drop, the Āditya.
The drop is the self.
14,18: "The gray-haired one has swallowed the young moon as it ran among the many;
behold the sage-like power of the god through his greatness! Today he dies, for he is the same as yesterday. (ṚV. 10.55.5) 14,18:
The gray-haired one—the Sun—swallows the young Moon, which is characterized by its dispersing nature (*vidhu*) and its waning nature (*dadrāṇa*).
"He dies immediately, as if risen during the day"—
thus with reference to the deities. Now, with reference to the self.
The one whose nature is to scatter the moon, the one whose nature is to subdue the fleeing youth—the Great One, whose self is gray-haired, swallows him;
he dies at night;
for the night has arrived.
14,18: Thus he declares the course of the Self.
14,19: "Of those born together, they call the seventh one single-born; the seers say there are six daughters of the gods.
Their desired abodes, established according to their stations, vibrate in manifold forms" (Ṛgveda 1.164.15).
Of the six rishis who were born together, the sun was the seventh.

Whatever they sacrificed to, whatever they desired, whatever they strode toward, whatever they attained, whatever they reflected upon, or whatever they bowed down to—all these things rejoice together with the waters.
Beyond those seven luminaries of the rishis lies the sun.
14.19: These become one in this [Self].
14.19: Thus with respect to the deities;
now with respect to the self.
Of the six faculties that are co-arisen, the self is the seventh. Whatever is desired, or beloved, or overcome, or gone, or thought, or bowed toward by these, they find delight together with food,
wherein these seven faculties of the seers reside.
Beyond these is the Supreme Self;
in Him they all become one.
He goes and declares the state of the Self.
"Those who are women, they call men to me; he who has eyes sees them, yet the blind man does not perceive them.
The son who is a seer (kavi) understands them; he who discerns them shall become the father of his father. (Ṛgveda 1.164.16).
These [objects] are indeed women, carrying away sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.

14.20: He who, fasting, perceives that "the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is that [breath] called 'male' (*puṃśabda*)," does not perceive sufferings, even though he is blind. The wise son is he who knows these;
he who knows these becomes the father of his father.
14.20: Thus he declares the course of the Self.
14.21: "The seven half-embryos, the seed of the world, abide by the command of Viṣṇu in the supporting law.
With their insights and with their mind, those wise ones, as all-pervading lords, encompass everything on every side" (Ṛgveda 1.164.36).
14,21: This Āditya swallows these seven rays of the Āditya; the word "upward" refers to his intermediate station.
14,21: Those [rays] which abide in him, he turns back through his insights (*dhīti*) and his mind.
14,21: As sovereigns, they encompass all ritual actions by means of the act of raining.
14.21: Thus with reference to the deities.
Now with reference to the self (*adhyātma*):
these seven sense-faculties this self swallows, [as indicated by] the word "middle" and "upward."
"Those [faculties] which abide in this [body], they are reversed by means of the intellect (*dhīti*) and the mind (*manas*).
As sovereigns, they overcome all the senses through knowledge and action. Thus he describes the movement of the Self.
14,22: "I do not know whether I am he or another; girt about, I move with my mind. When the first-born of Order come to me, then indeed I partake of a portion of this speech.
(ṚV 1,164,37) 14,22: I do not know whether I am he.
14.22: Hidden and firmly bound, I move about with the mind;
for one does not perceive it through the intellect. From this comes nourishment; they declare that the son is the self. This sun is the self. 14.23:
The out-breath goes forth, held by the *svadhā* offering; the immortal one has a common womb with the mortal.

"Those two, moving apart in opposite directions, go forever; people perceive one, but they do not perceive the other. (Ṛgveda 1.164.38) "The immortal Āditya, held by his own power, moves westward and moves eastward together with the mortal Moon.
They are those who go forever, who go everywhere, or who go in many ways.
14.23: He sees neither the sun nor the moon.
Thus with respect to the deities. Now with respect to the self.
14.23: He turns away and he turns toward, the immortal grasped by *svadhā*, together with the mortal mind.
These two go eternally, they go everywhere, they go in many ways. The self (*ātman*) sees itself, but the mind does not.
14,23: Thus he declares his own course.
14,24: "That indeed was the eldest among beings, from which the fierce one, of brilliant power, was born;
as soon as he was born, he struck down the enemies, he in whom all the helpers rejoice" (Ṛgveda 10.120.1).
14.24: "That exists as the eldest among beings and worlds, from whom the Āditya was born—fierce, with brilliant manly power, with radiant manly power.
As soon as he was born, he overcomes his enemies. Thus [it is said].
The root *niriṇāti* means either "to please" or "to illuminate," [as in the verse]: "Whom all the protectors (the Viśvedevas) rejoice in."
14.24: Thus with reference to the deities.
Now with reference to the self (adhyātma).
That occurs: among beings and worlds, the eldest, unmanifest, from which was born the fierce one, of brilliant valor, of the valor of knowledge.
14,24: "As soon as he is born, he overcomes his enemies.
14,24: The root *niriṇāti* means either the act of pleasing or the act of shining. 14,24: "Him all the *ūmas* rejoice after."
14,24: Thus he declares his own course.
14,25: "Who today yokes to the pole of the *ṛta* the vigorous, wrathful, and ill-disposed bulls?
Those who have arrows in their mouths and in their hearts, yet are sources of bliss—only he who fulfills their service shall live" (ṚV 1.84.16).
14,25: Ka yokes the oxen to the pole—the rays of the sun, which are active, radiant, and invincible; they bring forth the breaths and discharge the arrows that produce well-being and happiness?
He who knows this [breath] as thus gathered together—how does he live?
Thus with respect to the deities.

14.25: Now, with reference to the self. Who yokes the oxen to the pole? [The answer is: the senses, which are active, radiant, invincible, and which discharge arrows—the life-breaths—which discharge arrows and are sources of bliss, sources of happiness. He who knows these as they are gathered together lives for a long time.
14,25: Thus he declares the course of the Self. 14,26: "Who flees? Who is tormented? Who is afraid? Who perceives Indra as being near? 14,26:
Who will speak in favor of his offspring, his cattle, his wealth, and his own body, and for whom among the people? (Ṛgveda 1.84.17)
14,26: Who goes? Who gives? Who fears? Who honors the peaceful Indra?
Who [honors him] for our offspring, for our great joy, for that which is delightful and beautiful to behold?
14,27: Who shall kindle Agni with oblation and clarified butter? Who shall worship with the ladle according to the fixed seasons?
14,27: To whom shall the gods swiftly bring [offerings]? Who, as the one who performs the oblation, will be considered a true sacrificer and a god-favored host?

(Ṛgveda 1.84.18) 14,27: Who honors Āditya with the oblation and with clarified butter? Who shall sacrifice with the ladle according to the fixed seasons? 14,27: To whom shall the gods swiftly bring the objects intended for the oblation?
14.27: "Who will perceive him as the one who enjoys the oblation, the good god, the auspicious deity?
Thus with respect to the deities.
Now, with respect to the self.

14.27: Who honors himself with the oblation and with clarified butter, and who shall sacrifice with the ladle according to the fixed seasons? To whom have the gods brought those swift ones for the purpose of the offering?
Who, possessing the fire for the feast, shall deem himself wise, one of noble and auspicious insight?
14,27: Thus he declares his own course.
14,28: "O most powerful God, you indeed have praised the mortal;
O Maghavan Indra, there is no other comforter than you—I speak these words to you" (Ṛgveda 1.84.19).
14,28: O most powerful god, you alone indeed should praise the mortal man. 14,28: O Maghavan, there is no other than you who is a protector, a guardian, a victor, or one who brings happiness.
14,28: O Indra, I speak these words to you—words joined with praise.
14,29: "The swan dwelling in the pure [heaven], the Vasu dwelling in the intermediate space, the Hotṛ-priest dwelling at the altar, the guest dwelling in the house;

dwelling among men, dwelling in the best [of places], dwelling in Truth, dwelling in the sky; born of the waters, born of the kine, born of Truth, born of the mountains—He is the Truth. (Ṛgveda 4.40.5) 14,29:
"The swan," thus [it is said].
The swans are the rays of the sun;
the supreme self is the supreme light;
the earth is pervaded.
14,29: "Everything is pervaded; it is pervaded by the act of forest-dwelling through practice, like the solar disc.
14,29: "It transcends," thus says the world; "it transcends," thus [he says].
14,29: "The swan transcends."
14,29: The *haṃsas* are the *paramahaṃsas*.
14,29: The Supreme Self dwells in an abundant and profound abode by means of the rays of the sun; or rather, it dwells in three [abodes]. 14,29: Or, it dwells in three [states].
"Or: 'The ray dwells,' or 'The bearer dwells.

Suvarṇaretas (Golden-seeded), Pūṣan, the embryos—*ribhantā* means 'making them tremble' (*ribhantā vanakurilāni kurvantā*). *Ribhantā antarikṣā caratpathāntarikṣā cara* means 'moving through the paths of the atmosphere, moving through the atmosphere. Or it refers to movement in heaven and on earth. *Subhānuḥ suprabhūtaḥ hotā ādityasya gatā bhavanti* means 'the Hotṛ of the Sun, possessing beautiful luster and abundant power, becomes those who have gone. *Atithir duroṇasat*—all [beings] dwell in the house; all juices draw themselves together. The ray draws them together."
14,29: Fire draws [the world] apart;
it becomes a forest.
Horses, cattle, mountain-born cattle, earth-born cattle—all these are born of the cow; they are born of Truth (*ṛta*) and possess many sounds.
14,29: The *nigama* (Vedic citations) and the *nigamavyatibhāva* (the intermingling of citations) serve for the purpose of etymological explanation (*nirvacana*).
14,30: "Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree.
One of them eats the sweet fruit; the other looks on without eating" (Ṛgveda 1.164.20).
14.30: Two by two they stand established, performers of righteous deeds (*dharmakartṛ*).
They call the evil deed "sin" (*pāpa*) and "that which surrounds" (*parisāraka*).
With the verse, "The two fair-winged ones, yoked together, companions," he rises toward the Supreme Self from the individual self (*ātman*).
14.30: That [immortality] is born indeed within the body.
One protects the tree, the body; one establishes the two wings upon the tree.
Having eaten the food of one of these two, while not eating the other, he who knows thus attains similarity of form and residence in the same world.
"Another, not eating, looks on"—thus he declares the course of the Self. "Come, O Indra, by the paths invoked; enjoy this our sacrifice as your allotted portion."
14,31: "They have abandoned her who is satisfied, like a wife to her maternal uncle, or like the portion of the daughter of one's father’s sister, or like the omentum.

14,31: "The gods, including Śakra, shall come; by these three celebrated fords, the Śakra-fords, may you accept this sacrifice of ours, this sacrificial portion, and the portions of Agni and Soma; may Indra enjoy them. 14,31: "Thus satisfied, she is like the portion of a maternal uncle’s daughter joined with a husband; those who are the deities stand in that place, and Śakra is the illustration thereof."
14,32: "The wise ones call upon the wise one for protection; mortals call upon the god Agni with songs for assistance" (Ṛgveda 8.11.6).
14,32: The wise ones know the wise one for protection.
14,32: That which is to be known is found through the Vedas.

14,32: By means of the wind within the stainless body, the wise man should fill the letter *U*—which resides within the lotus of the heart and is joined with the letter *A*—until it reaches the abode of the letter *M*. This wise one, sprinkled with the *bindu* among the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), is blossomed, possesses the radiance of the fire-god’s splendor, has an immortal body within golden lotuses, and dwells in that which is born of immortality; they declare him to be the Truth (*ṛta*) in the mouth of those whose speech is immortal.
14,32: "We invoke Agni with songs.
14,32: One should awaken Agni [with the thought]: "Agni is all the deities. 14,32:
The following verse serves for his further explanation.
14,33: "Let us press the Soma for Jātavedas; he burns up the possessions of the one who acts with hostility.
May Agni carry us across all difficulties, as if across a river in a boat, beyond all misfortunes.
(Ṛgveda 1,99,1) 14,33: "For Jātavedas," thus [it is said].

14,33: "All this, moving and unmoving, has been born according to the principle of maintenance, origination, and dissolution; let us press the Soma"—with this impulse for the pressing, [the priest] places King Soma, the nectar, for the sake of the sacrifice against the one who acts with hostility. "Sma" expresses certainty. He burns, he consumes, he reduces to ashes; the meaning is that Soma gives.

14,33: May he carry us across difficulties—difficult places—as one who is skilled at steering a boat carries a ship across the ocean, or as a helmsman carries a boat across a river that is difficult to traverse, with its great banks and turbulent waters; [Agni] carries us across misfortunes (*duritāni*).
Regarding this, there is another verse:
14,34: "This [offering] of yours is unequalled by other waters, whatever rivers flow toward the Sindhu."
14,34: "Having approached with his head, he casts off evil like a snake sheds its worn-out skin.
14,34: "This [water] of yours is distinct from those other rivers which flow making the Sindhu their lord.
14,34: "The serpent abandons its skin like a snake sheds its worn-out skin."
14.34: They abandon evil.
14.34: [The word] *āpaḥ* is derived from the root *āp* (to obtain).
14.34: Regarding them, this [verse] occurs.
14,35: "We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity.
May I be liberated from death like a cucumber from its stem, yet not be separated from immortality.
(Ṛgveda 7.59.12) 14,35: Tryambaka is Rudra; we worship that Tryambaka, the fragrant one.
14,35: Fragrant, of excellent fragrance;
14,35: like that which increases nourishment, a producer of prosperity;
14,35: like the fruit of the cucumber, release me from my bond, from the presence of death.
Because there is a subsequent [verse] for these others:
14,36: "Live a hundred autumns, increasing in prosperity; a hundred winters, and a hundred springs."
"May Indra, Agni, Savitṛ, and Bṛhaspati restore this man through the hundred-lived oblation" (ṚV 10.161.4).
There is also a Vedic citation: "Live for a hundred autumns, growing in strength.
Here, "a hundred" refers to a long life of a hundred years.
14,36: The Maruts cause him to increase by this. 14,36: He becomes possessed of a hundredfold self, even as a hundredfold self;
he becomes a hundredfold, which is infinite.
14,36: There is a hundredfold sovereignty.
"A hundred" means a hundred long years of life. 14,37:
"O Vasu, may your gifts and your aids never fail us at any time."

O Manava, measure out for us all riches for the sake of the people. Let not your abodes, nor any of your powers, ever fail us. All forms of wisdom are for the purpose of comparison, for the benefit of humanity.
14,37: This sun is this self. 14,37: Now they recite this [hymn] accordingly. 14,37: Now this collection of Ṛg-verses proclaims this great self for Vaiśvakarman.
14,37: “Now we shall declare the births of the gods,” and also: “At that time, there was neither non-being nor being.
This is that inquiry into the Self.
14,37: This is the inquiry into all beings.
He who knows this is led by Brahman to the state of being most similar to it, to having the same form as it, and to dwelling in the same world as it.
Homage to Brahman!
Homage to the Great Being!
Homage to Pāraskara!
